docs.title: The Aging Manual
docs.text:
What you, or your parents, do next.

A practical manual for ordinary people in China: how the body ages, what to check, what to ask for, and who to ask. It does not teach you how to grow old — it asks only that you can find the right page when something goes wrong.

Read in Chinese (中文版) GitHub repository

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
In China there is no shortage of books about growing old. What is missing is the one you can follow. Translations of good foreign books — Being Mortal, The Book About Getting Older — talk about attitude and conversation, but their institutions, money and paperwork are foreign. Official materials are authoritative and free, but they sit scattered across dozens of documents from a dozen departments, one document to one subject, and none of them is written in language a reader can use.

This manual tries to close that gap: Chinese context, the whole arc of aging, an evidence grade and an official entry point on every entry, open source and correctable. It is arranged by the four stages of aging — build your reserves; read the warning signs; arrange the home, the money and the people; then the last stretch.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
Every entry follows the same shape: what it costs, in short, what you can do, where this comes from, who this is for, what you get back, and — for the Chinese system — how this works in China.

Every figure carries a grade: A means a specific, publicly checkable source; B means research support without an exact figure; C means common practice, not evidence. Where a source is second-hand it is marked second-hand; where we could not check it at all, unverified. There is no dose, no prescription and no diagnosis anywhere in this book — only who to ask and what to ask.

docs.title: Chapter 0 · How to use this manual
Who wrote this
docs.text:
Not a doctor.

It was put together with the help of AI: the public material was read through, the official documents were checked one by one, and what was left was sorted out. So nothing in here comes from an experiment of ours — this book contains no measurements of our own. Every number carries a grade tag saying where it came from and how strong that source is, so you can open it and check for yourself; where we could not check it, we say so.

Nor does this book set out to teach you how to grow old. The people who wrote it are aging too. They forget things, they find things a nuisance, and there are things they would rather not face.

docs.title: This is not a checklist
docs.text:
You may open it and feel tense: so many entries, and you can't manage one of them.

You don't have to. Of all the entries in this book, you will use two or three in a lifetime. Pick one or two and do them, and the book has paid for itself. Leave the rest for reference: come back to them when you, or your parents, actually reach that point.

That is why it looks like a manual and not a textbook. A manual never asks you to read it from cover to cover. It only asks that you can find the right page when something goes wrong.

docs.title: Four accounts, not one
docs.text:
This book wants to help you keep four accounts:

  • Independence — eating, using the toilet, washing, going out on your own; and being able to get things done on a phone (booking an appointment, hailing a ride, paying)
  • Money — your own retirement money, and the money your children get pulled into
  • Relationships — your partner, your children, old friends, neighbours, the community. What runs out first in old age is often not the body but the relationships
  • Dignity — not being humoured like a child, not losing your composure in front of people, still making your own decisions

These four accounts cannot pay for each other. One fewer fall does not buy you an extra 300 yuan a month, and an extra 300 yuan a month will not buy back a fall you didn't take. Neither stands in for the other.

This comes first because most books about aging keep only one account: how long you live, or how much you spend. Keep one account and you end up concluding "this is better than that"; keep four, and you find that many things do not need comparing at all — they are simply different things.

docs.title: How to read each entry
docs.text:
Most entries have a fixed shape:

  • What it costs: what this item takes out of you — money, time, effort, and whether you have to bring something up. Aging has a peculiarity: the most expensive cost is often not money but being unable to say the thing out loud. So "whether you have to bring it up" gets a line of its own.
  • In short: what this is actually about. After reading this line you should be able to explain it to your partner or your children.
  • What you can do: actions you can follow. Only the method — nothing forces you to do it.
  • Where this comes from: where the entry came from. A = a public source with a specific checkable figure (systematic review, large study, the text of a statute); B = supported by research, but no exact figure available (a single small study, for instance); C = common practice and experience, not evidence. If you are unsure, follow the letter back.
  • Who this is for: who the entry holds true for. A healthy 60-year-old and an 80-year-old with several chronic conditions need different things.
  • The last two lines: What you get back (which of the four accounts this pays into, and which fear it removes), and How this works in China (who to ask, where to go, what subsidies exist).

Some entries have only three lines. If one sentence says it clearly, we don't pad the format.

docs.title: Two paths
docs.text:
Path one: for yourself. Match yourself first — which stage of aging are you at?

  • Stage 1 Not old yet (forty or fifty, or you still think of yourself as young): build up your reserves. Go to Part 1.
  • Stage 2 Just starting to age (your body has begun sending signals): read the signals, get what should be checked. Go to Part 2.
  • Stage 3 Starting to need help (your strength is going, or there is someone disabled at home): sort out the home, the money, the people. Go to Part 4.
  • Stage 4 The last stretch: how to have the conversations, how to make the arrangements. Go to Part 5.

You can also skip the stages and look things up directly: Appendix B is arranged by physical symptom (pain, leaking, forgetting, falling), Appendix C by what you are afraid of (of getting poor, of burdening your children, of loneliness, of dying in pain).

Path two: for your parents. Start with Chapter 20, "How to start the conversation". Your hardest problem is usually not that you don't know how to prevent a fall — it is that you don't know how to say it to them. Then look things up by symptom or by fear. Finally, read the section at the end of each chapter, "If you are reading this for a parent". It covers what you can do first, when they are not in the room or will not admit to anything.

docs.title: If you have ten minutes
docs.text:
Do these three now. They cost nothing, or very little:

  1. Take the mats out of the bathroom and the entryway. Not put them away — take them out of the house. These are the two places where older people fall most, and a mat is the most common thing to trip on.
  2. Tonight, put motion-sensor night lights along the route from bed to toilet. Thirty to eighty yuan. Most people's problem is not that they have no light, but that they have one light, not a path.
  3. Photograph everything you take — medicine and supplements both. Keep it on your phone under the name "my medicine". Next time you see a doctor, show it to them. That is the first thing a doctor wants to know, and you will usually not be able to list it all from memory.

docs.title: When this book does not apply
docs.text:
• Emergencies: chest pain, unable to speak, one side of the body not moving, confusion. Call 120. Chapter 8 has a one-page table for judgement; don't read it now, turn to it when something happens.
  • Once you have a diagnosis: this book is about preparing and arranging. It does not replace your doctor. Which treatment to take is a question for the doctor who is treating you.
  • About medicine: this book gives no doses and no prescriptions. Only who to go to and what to ask.

docs.title: One honest thing
docs.text:
Some things this book cannot fix. Disability, the loss of a spouse, and the last thing of all — it cannot hold any of them back.

What it can do is turn "caught off guard" into "arranged in advance". That difference often changes a person's last years more than curing any single disease.

docs.title: Foreword · Older people are our future selves
You may have picked this up for a parent, or for yourself
docs.text:
The two read completely differently.

People reading it for a parent are in a hurry to find "what do we do"; they will be disappointed if the book holds nothing they can act on. People reading it for themselves mostly noticed something in their own body — a raised white-cell count on one blood test, breathless on the stairs once, a moment of blackout standing up from a squat.

This book serves both. The main text talks to "you"; at the end of every chapter there is a section called "If you are reading this for a parent".

docs.title: Three numbers, not one
docs.text:
Past sixty, everyone hears the same number: life expectancy. It tells you roughly how many years you have.

But what actually decides whether the last years go well are two other numbers:

  • Healthy life expectancy — the years without major illness, in which you look after yourself
  • Years of independence — the years in which you can eat, use the toilet, wash and go out on your own

The last one matters most. It is "freedom" itself: only if you can go out alone does "where to go" even arise; only if you can use the toilet alone does dignity arise.

So this book is not about living long. It is about pushing the number of independent years back. China has no stable official figure for "years of independence" yet; Chapter 1 sets out where things stand. The number probably differs between north and south, between city and countryside.

docs.title: Growing old does not happen in one day
docs.text:
Most people feel they got old all at once. It wasn't that moment.

The body runs a system of compensation: when one function declines, the rest take on more. That system is tough, and it can cover your weak spots for years. So you don't feel the decline — until one day it can't hold: a fall, a hospital stay, an infection.

That moment is not the start of aging. It is the day the lid came off.

Which is why this book wants you to read it now. Not because something will happen to you today, but because on the day it does happen, the notes you reach for should not be someone else's.

docs.title: Compression of morbidity: squeezing the hard stretch shorter
docs.text:
Geriatric medicine has a term for it: compression of morbidity.

It means illness and disability will not disappear; what we can do is postpone them and squeeze them shorter. Turn "the hard years" from ten into three, from lying down into still going out on your own.

The goal doesn't sound ambitious, but it is far more practical than living to a hundred.

docs.title: Older people are our future selves
docs.text:
The line is not this book's invention. It comes from Lucy Pollock: "Our parents and grandparents look at us, and their faces say, 'Here I am, your future.'" (Lucy Pollock, The Book About Getting Older (for people who don't want to talk about it), Penguin Books, 2020, ch. 2, p. 24). Chinese edition: Lucy Pollock, 《变老之前要知道》, translated by 一熙, Guangdong People's Publishing House, "万有引力" imprint; bibliographic record https://book.douban.com/subject/38368536/ ; see also 郭晔旻, 《变老之前要知道的那些事》, China Science Daily, 21 August 2026, https://news.sciencenet.cn/sbhtmlnews/2026/8/390983.shtm

Pollock is a British geriatrician who worked on geriatric wards for more than thirty years. What she describes is a shift of standpoint.

"Treat the elders of others as your own" treats older people as other people, who deserve our kindness. Treating yourself as a future older person is admitting that this, too, is a stretch of your own life, that you will live inside it — and that you should therefore start arranging for that self now.

This book is written from the second standpoint. It was shaped by two things. One is the attitude of Pollock's book — the hard part is not the answer, it is saying it out loud (her own words: fear and prejudice mix into 'a toxic mix that kills conversations', ch. 2, p. 25, our translation). The other is an open-source project, HowToLiveBetter (GitHub: eternity4719/HowToLiveBetter), which tags every suggestion with its cost, its benefit, its evidence level and its original source. We borrowed both: the attitude from the book, the format from the project — but none of its numbers.

docs.title: The anxiety business
docs.text:
Aging is the easiest topic of all to be harvested in. The reason is not complicated: many people are afraid, information is unevenly spread, and judgement drops when you are frightened.

So someone will sell you a medical check-up package for several thousand yuan and say it catches everything early; someone will sell you a "memory-enhancing" supplement and say it prevents dementia; someone will take your property deed and say you can collect rent lying down.

This book's method against that is crude: every entry carries its source, and anything we could not check we would rather leave out. Where a fear is being used by sellers, we mark it separately (see the table below).

docs.title: The things people fear most about aging, and how this book meets them
docs.text:
The table below names those fears one by one. The second column says whether the fear is well placed — some are justified, some point in the wrong direction, and some are being used by sellers.

What you fear Is the fear well placed? Where to look One fall and it's over Justified. A fall really is the turning point of later life, but it is preventable, and the most useful measures together cost less than a few hundred yuan Chapter 5 Wetting yourself and being found out Justified, but you mostly don't have to put up with it. Most cases can be improved; putting up with it is what actually loses you face Chapter 10 Forgetting things — is it dementia? Wrong direction. There is a wide gap between normal forgetting and disease, and plenty you can do in between Chapter 9 Something happens at home alone at night and no one knows Justified. But it can be arranged: one-touch alarms, scheduled check-ins, a living-alone agreement Chapter 15 Your partner goes first, and the days after Justified, and no one can prepare it for you. But the supports in your daily life can be built in advance Chapter 22 Getting old just means spending money and suffering Wrong direction. Spending has an order — spend the few hundred first, not the tens of thousands Chapters 12, 16 You will certainly be put in a care home by your children Mostly not. But if you don't say anything, your children will decide for you. That is the real problem Chapter 20 Being a burden on your children Justified. Which is why nearly half of this book is about making sure you don't need looking after Part 4 Being left behind because you can't do things on a phone Justified. But it is learnable, not a matter of ability. Booking appointments, hailing rides, paying, topping up utilities — each can be learned Chapter 18 Being scammed Justified. Scammers now swap faces, clone voices and pose as customer service, and they call when you are alone at home Chapter 18 Dying in pain, without dignity Justified. And it can be arranged in advance — many people simply don't know that Chapter 21 "If you don't get this checked it will be too late" / "this prevents dementia" A fear being used by sellers. Expensive check-up packages and "memory-enhancing" supplements mostly cannot show evidence Chapters 1, 12

The table is here so that you can first say the fear out loud clearly. Naming a fear is not the same as frightening you: every line pairs the fear with whether it is well placed, and with a chapter that meets it.

A few of them point in the wrong direction, and that is not your fault. Nobody taught us this thirty years ago.

docs.title: One honest thing
docs.text: Nobody can give you a painless answer about aging. What this book can do is turn most of what is in it from "dropped on you suddenly" into "already thought about, and a little prepared for".

docs.title: About this material, and what it does not take on
docs.text:
This is not a commissioned book and it is not an institutional project.

It began with something small: as I got older, I wanted to know for myself — what to watch for after a fall, how a tableful of medicines should actually be sorted, how far I can stand in for my parents when they can't get things done on a phone, and who to go to for which procedure when that day comes. I went looking, and found the material is all there, just scattered: half of it on government and hospital websites, half of it in guidelines and journals, the rest in news reports — and with a fair amount of it contradicting itself.

With AI to help, it can now be put together quickly into the manual you are reading. It was written to the standard of "I will need this myself later": every entry has to have a source you can check; where it does not, it says "not found" — no fudging, not even for myself.

Having looked it all up anyway, it seemed better to put it out. There are probably plenty of people who need it the way I did, and every one who can be saved the work is worth it. Hence this open-source collection of material.

docs.title: Read these few lines first
docs.text:
This is not medical advice. I don't see patients and I don't prescribe. There is not one dose, not one prescription, not one diagnosis in this book. Wherever it differs from what your doctor says, follow the doctor in front of you who has seen you in person. In an emergency call 120 first, don't reach for a book.

This is not legal advice. Guardianship, wills, inheritance, signatures — practice varies a lot by locality, and the regulations keep changing. This book tells you only that the thing exists, roughly which window to ask at, and which questions to ask. For how it actually works, ask a notary office, a lawyer, or the department in charge.

This is not investment advice. I recommend no products and comment on no financial product's merits. The money-related parts of this book cover two things only: how the state's systems work, and how people cheat you.

The policies and figures in here are dated. Every source carries the date I checked it (broadly, October 2026). Policies get adjusted, phone numbers change, guidelines are updated. Before you act, check again yourself using the leads in the book, or call 12345 / 12333 and ask. Anything marked unverified is a place where I could not reach the original document — treat that claim with care.

Where I am not sure, I say so. There are more than two hundred such notes across the book, all listed in each chapter's closing section. These are not boilerplate disclaimers; they are places where I genuinely could not check. If you find the source, I would be glad to hear it; if you find an error, more glad still.

docs.title: Whether to act on it is your call
docs.text:
All this book can do is lay out what was found, and where it came from. Whether to act on it, you know better than I do: your illness, your medicines, your family, how much money and time you have.

For anything involving medication, exercise, diet or care arrangements, ask a doctor first. For anything involving signatures, property or guardianship, ask a lawyer or a notary first. If you do something because this book said so, the outcome is yours to carry.

docs.title: One last line
docs.text:
This is something I looked up and sorted out for my own use with the help of AI, put out in passing for others to consult. It does not replace your judgement, and it does not tell you how to live.

Take what is useful, turn past what is not.

docs.title: Chapter 1 · Growing Old Does Not Happen in One Day
docs.text:
You are probably somewhere like this. In your forties, and for the first time your checkup report has an extra arrow or two next to it, and you laugh it off with "I've reached that age"; or in your fifties, and when you squat down and stand back up, you have to pause in place for half a second before you dare take a step.

You have not yet counted yourself among the "old". But you are already counting, in your head: how many more years can I go downstairs on my own, go out on my own, make my own decisions.

Where you stand in the process of getting old right now decides what you should be saving up over the next ten years.

Stage Where you are now What to do at this stage Which part to turn to Stage one: not old yet In your forties or fifties, or you still consider yourself young Save up capital: muscle, bone, heart and brain, and also money and people Part One Stage two: just starting to get old Your body begins to send signals: blood pressure is up, stairs leave you short of breath, your back gives out Read the signals; get checked for what should be checked; prevent what should be prevented Part Two Stage three: starting to need help Your strength is failing, or there is someone disabled at home Sort out the home, the money, the people, the authority Part Four Stage four: the last stretch The days have gone into countdown Open up the conversation; put the final decisions in writing Part Five

This book is written stage by stage. You are most likely in Stage One, or just stepping out of Stage One into Stage Two. This chapter is written for people in Stage One.

docs.title: 1.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
Most people only start thinking about their later years after an accident: a fall, a hospital stay, a family member noticing that you can't remember things.

By the time that day comes, half of what you could have done is already out of reach.

This chapter, while nothing has gone wrong yet, sets three things out clearly. First, how getting old happens: it starts at thirty, you just can't feel it. Second, "old" is not one thing but four different things, and many people use these four words interchangeably — and once they are mixed up, what should have been prevented hasn't been prevented, and what should have been checked hasn't been checked. Third, which of the things called "just age" are actually illnesses to be treated, and which fears are being sold to you by someone.

docs.title: 1.2 The body has a lid, and it can hold things down for years
docs.text:
Growing old does not happen in one day. That sentence has two layers.

One layer is that the downward slope starts very early, a little each year, not suddenly on some day.

The other layer is that the body has a set of compensatory mechanisms: when one function declines, other places take on more of the load, and they can hold a hidden problem down for many years. So you don't notice that it is declining.

Until one day the lid can no longer hold: a fall, an infection, a hospital stay. That moment is not the starting point of getting old; it is the day the lid is lifted off.

This is why you should read this book now. Not because something will happen to you today, but because if you wait until the day it happens to open it, the notebook you open should have been in someone else's hands.

docs.title: 1.3 The slide starts at thirty
docs.text:
Three things were already going downhill before you felt old.

Muscle. Muscle mass peaks between twenty and the late thirties, then starts to decline. One set of studies gives the numbers: after adulthood, men lose about 4.7% per decade and women about 3.7% (note: these figures come from research cited by the Hong Kong government's Department of Health, not a mainland population; for the mainland there is still no unified set of curves by age and by sex) official wording Hong Kong SAR Government, Department of Health. What falls faster than muscle mass is muscle strength: in the same set of studies, men lose 14.5% per decade and women lose 11.8% official wording Hong Kong SAR Government, Department of Health. In other words, you don't first get "thin" — you first run out of strength.

Bone. Bone keeps growing until around thirty, when bone mass reaches its highest point, called peak bone mass in medicine; after thirty to thirty-five, bone mass starts to decline official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission. The higher your peak bone mass, the later problems appear. Among people over fifty in China, the prevalence of osteoporosis is 19.2% — 32.1% in women and 6.9% in men official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission.

Heart and lungs. The body's ability to use oxygen is usually measured by maximal oxygen uptake. It falls with age, and falls faster and faster: in your twenties and thirties it drops 3% to 6% per decade, and after seventy it drops more than 20% per decade third-party research Fleg et al., 2005.

Put the three together and they are the same sentence: it is not "getting old suddenly one day" but "a little less every year", accumulating to some number before it becomes visible.

docs.title: 1.4 Getting old is not one thing; it comes in four models
docs.text:
"Old" is too broad a word. In geriatric medicine, four things each have their own name; they do different things and take different paths.

  • Frailty: the whole person's reserves get thin, and the capacity to withstand a blow is poor.
  • Sarcopenia: the muscle, as an organ, is wasting away.
  • Multimorbidity: not one disease, but a string of diseases existing at the same time.
  • Disability: function has already been lost; help is needed.

These four push each other along, but if they are bundled into one "getting old", a signal that could still be caught and intervened on early gets taken for an unsalvageable outcome.

docs.title: Frailty: one small illness floors you
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing in normal times; to get it properly checked you add one outpatient visit (Money: barely any money | Time: a few minutes | Effort: nothing | Do you have to speak up: no)
  • In short: the same cold, the same minor operation — others ride it out, you don't, and you recover very slowly. This is frailty: not that some organ has broken, but that the whole person's margin has got thin.
  • How to judge (against the numbers): ① without dieting, you have lost 5% of your weight in six months (someone weighing 100 jin loses 5 jin); ② you often feel weak and tired; ③ your grip strength has dropped — you can't twist open a bottle cap or carry groceries; ④ you walk more slowly than people your age; ⑤ your activity has clearly fallen off, and you don't want to move anything. Three of these five usually count as frailty; one or two of them is called "pre-frailty" third-party research Fried frailty phenotype.
  • Who this is for: it holds for you if you can still get by on your own, just with a thin margin. Frailty does not equal being bedridden; it is the stretch before being bedridden, and part of that stretch can be walked back.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid that "one small illness and I never get up again"

docs.title: Sarcopenia: first you lose strength, then you lose power
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing in normal times; if you want a confirmed diagnosis, add one outpatient visit plus tests
  • In short: sarcopenia is not "thin". It means the amount and the strength of your muscle have fallen to a point where they already affect your walking, standing up, and carrying things.
  • How to work it out: the Asian diagnostic criteria for sarcopenia (AWGS 2019) give several lines. Grip strength, below 28 kg for men and below 18 kg for women; walking speed, slower than 1.0 m/s; standing up from a chair five times in a row, over 12 seconds; calf circumference, below 34 cm for men and below 33 cm for women third-party research AWGS 2019. What you can do at home first: measure your calf circumference, see whether twisting off a bottle cap is hard work, and count whether you need to push off with your hands to get up out of a chair.
  • One number: the prevalence of sarcopenia among older people in China, pooling 22 papers, is about 14.6% third-party research meta-analysis, 2022; looking at individual studies on their own, because the diagnostic criteria and the sampled populations differ, figures from single digits to thirty percent have been reported (8.9%–38.8% in community studies, reaching 67.1% among those over eighty) third-party research Chinese Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Sarcopenia in Older Adults, 2021.
  • Who this is for: it holds for you if — your weight isn't necessarily low, you may look normal or even a bit heavy, but your muscle is quietly shrinking (this is called "sarcopenic obesity"). So don't judge by the scale.
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid that "my legs have no strength, I can't walk far or stand for long"
  • How this works in China: to get assessed, register with geriatrics, rehabilitation medicine, or general practice; a contracted family doctor at a community health centre can also do an initial screening. Programmes and fees differ from place to place, so go by the latest local rules.

docs.title: Multimorbidity: not one disease but a string of them
docs.text:
• What it costs: no money, just the time for one extra visit (Do you have to speak up: easy enough, you just have to admit your illnesses aren't few)
  • In short: having two or more chronic diseases at the same time is called multimorbidity. The trouble is not how severe any one disease is, but that they and their respective medicines fight each other.
  • How to work it out: count the chronic diseases you have already been diagnosed with; two or more, and that is multimorbidity. Among people over sixty in China, the self-reported multimorbidity rate is about 43.6% (CHARLS 2015, 11,707 people) third-party research; if you also count the results of checkups and lab tests, the proportion is much higher — across the same dataset the 2011 and 2015 waves are 85.96% and 92.24% respectively third-party research. The two figures differ so widely only on "which diseases count".
  • Who this is for: it holds for people with more than one illness and more than one medicine. The most practical single move for multimorbidity: each time you see a doctor, remind them once that "I'm still taking medicine prescribed for another condition" (see Chapter 6).
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid that "the more the illnesses are treated, the more there are, and the more medicine I take, the more muddled it gets"

docs.title: Disability: function is already gone
docs.text:
• What it costs: no money, just one conversation about care
  • In short: among these six things — eating, dressing, bathing, using the toilet, getting in and out of bed, moving about indoors — if one of them needs help over the long term, that is disability; the more of them need help, the more severe it is.
  • How to work it out: count how many of those six need help. Then go on to count the "instrumental" ones: going out to buy groceries, taking transport, paying bills, using a phone to get things done. In China, "being able to get things done on a phone" is also counted as part of independence (see Chapter 0).
  • One number: according to the National Health Commission, China has more than 45 million older people who are disabled or have dementia, roughly one in every six older people needing long-term care official wording National Health Commission. (A note on the scope: the 45 million is disability plus dementia; counting only disabled older people, there is another figure of about 35 million — see the sources for Chapter 4.)
  • Who this is for: it holds for people who already need a hand. Once you reach this point, the focus of the conversation changes: it is no longer "how to prevent it", but "who will care for me, where the money comes from, how to keep my dignity" (turn to Part Four).
  • What you get back: independence — no longer afraid that "one day I'll even need to be fed" Remember the one distinction between the four words: frailty is a thin margin; sarcopenia is muscle shrinking; multimorbidity is many diseases; disability is function lost.

docs.title: 1.5 "Compression of morbidity": making the hard years shorter
docs.text:
In geriatric medicine there is a term called compression of morbidity. In 1980 the American physician James Fries proposed it third-party research Fries, 1980: total lifespan has a ceiling; what you can do is push the period of illness and disability later and compress it shorter.

Living long is lifespan; living well is health span — these are two different numbers.

China's average life expectancy was 79 years in 2024, and 79.25 years at the end of 2025 official wording National Health Commission. As for "the years you can get by on your own, without depending on others", the National Health Commission's annual bulletin does not carry that figure — the bulletin publishes only average life expectancy, and does not list "healthy life expectancy" separately; the World Health Organization has its own estimates for each country, but it uses a different method, so you cannot simply subtract one from the other. So this chapter does not lay out two numbers for you to subtract; it states one certain thing: for the extra years you live, whether you can get by on your own or are lying there needing care — the difference is right there.

If the extra years cannot be lived independently, then "longevity" becomes "a longer stretch of suffering". What compression of morbidity wants is for "two or three hard years" to take the place of "ten hard years".

docs.title: 1.6 Five misconceptions, the first is the most dangerous
Misconception one: "It's just age, it's normal"
docs.text:
This sentence is the most expensive one. Some changes are aging, some are illness; sweeping them all under "getting old" amounts to letting a treatable illness drag on until it is untreatable.

The following things are often taken for "just age" when they should be investigated.

  • Getting weaker and weaker, feeling cold, constipation, poor memory, low mood: could be hypothyroidism. In a survey of 78,470 cases across 31 provinces in China, subclinical hypothyroidism was the most common among older people, with a prevalence close to 20% third-party research Chinese Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Thyroid Disease in Older Adults, 2021.
  • Dizziness, a pale face, breathlessness at the slightest movement: could be anaemia. Anaemia is common in older people, yet it is often taken for normal aging, or hidden behind other chronic diseases official wording Beijing Municipal Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
  • Breathless after two steps, waking at night gasping, swollen ankles: could be heart failure.
  • No energy, not wanting to do anything, waking early: could be depression, not something that "cheering up" will fix. Among middle-aged and older people aged 45 and over in China, the detection rate of depressive symptoms is 23.61% (CFPS, 2018) third-party research Journal of Sichuan University (Medical Sciences), 2021.
  • Losing weight over six months, no appetite: get it checked; don't treat it as "getting thin in old age".

Remember a formulation that is hard to get wrong: a single change that has appeared only in the last few months, and is still moving in the wrong direction, is not "slow aging" — it is something to be looked at. Conversely, something that appears suddenly within days (can't speak clearly, weakness on one side, chest pain) is not a matter of "having it looked at", but a matter of calling 120 (see Chapter 8).

  • Who this is for: everyone. This one does not depend on age.

docs.title: Misconception two: "You can't buy a thin old age for a thousand pieces of gold"
docs.text:
• In short: once you are old, losing weight is not necessarily a good thing — what you lose is mostly muscle. What you should watch is muscle, not the number on the scale.
  • What you can do: stop looking only at weight. If you have lost more than 5% of your weight in six months (the threshold is in the frailty item in 1.4), see a doctor about why, rather than being pleased.

docs.title: Misconception three: brain supplements prevent dementia
docs.text:
• In short: so far, no health product has been proven to prevent dementia or improve memory. What actually helps the brain is controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, exercise and social contact, and fixing hearing problems.
  • What you can do: if you're willing to spend money, spend it on these first; hold off on the supplements.

docs.title: Misconception four: "When you're old you should move less and rest"
docs.text:
• In short: the less you move, the faster muscle and heart-lung function fall away, and the more likely you are to fall. Deciding to stop moving because you're afraid of falling is the worst option (see Chapter 5).
  • What you can do: start with what you can do, even if it's lifting your legs while sitting, or practising standing up while holding on to something.

docs.title: Misconception five: "After eighty, checkups are pointless"
docs.text:
• In short: it's neither do everything nor do nothing. What you should do is the handful of screenings picked out for your age, physical condition, and risk. Picking out that handful is exactly the job geriatrics and the checkup report should do (see Chapter 14).
  • What you can do: replace "should I have this test" with "will this change how I'm treated"; if the answer is no, don't have it.

docs.title: 1.7 Who makes money off your fear
docs.text:
Aging is the topic easiest to harvest, and some people call it the "anxiety business". Why it is fertile ground: there are many people who are afraid, you don't understand, the seller does, and people's judgement drops when they are frightened; and people living alone have one fewer person to talk things over with.

To deal with it, this book has only one dumb method: write a source for every item; and mark out separately every "fear that is exploited by sellers".

docs.title: Expensive checkup packages, and "one drop of blood"
docs.text:
• In short: proper cancer screening is done separately, by risk, one cancer one test. Low-dose CT for the lungs, colonoscopy for the bowel, mammography or ultrasound for the breast. Anything that claims in one sentence to "screen for all cancers" or "screen for a hundred diseases" is selling a gimmick. The claim "one drop of blood tests for cancer" has been debunked repeatedly; the American company that made it its headline product, its founder was ultimately sentenced to 11 years 3 months in prison for fraud official wording U.S. Department of Justice announcement, 2022-11-18.
  • How to spot it: when words like "test everything at once", "predict", "premium", "genetic" appear, put a question mark on them first. Renaming routine items and marking up the price is standard practice in this trade.
  • What happens if you don't buy: you save a few thousand yuan and are missing nothing. But remember: don't save on the screenings you should have along with it. The few that really should be done are set by a doctor according to your situation.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "spending a bit buys peace of mind"

docs.title: Brain supplements and health-product seminars
docs.text:
• In short: in the cases published by the State Administration for Market Regulation, the chain of scams in older people's health products is a fixed four steps: free trials, manufacturing anxiety, false advertising, high-price sales official wording State Administration for Market Regulation.
  • How to spot it: be on your guard against anyone who has you collect something free, sit through a seminar, join a group chat, or watch a livestream first. Many of those "the effect is really good, I'll order two more months" buyers in the group are shills. A common food or health product claiming to cure disease is itself illegal advertising.
  • What happens if you don't buy: you save money and time. The treatment you should have won't be any less for it, and you were never relying on it for treatment in the first place.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "I have to do something for my health"

docs.title: Housing-for-pension
docs.text:
• In short: the thing being piloted by the state is properly called "reverse mortgage pension insurance", an insurance product. The scam borrows the policy's name to get you to mortgage your home and take the money to invest in "high-interest wealth products" official wording National Financial Regulatory Administration risk notice.
  • How to spot it: whenever someone wants you to sign to mortgage your property in order to invest, however much the name looks like a policy, it is a scam. In the legitimate version the house is still yours, you draw money monthly and it is dealt with after your death; the terms and rights must be asked through point by point.
  • What happens if you don't buy: the house is still there, and you are still living in it. For most families this matters far more than the extra bit of interest.
  • What you get back: money + dignity — no longer afraid that "there isn't enough money and I'll lose my life savings" One general rule: whenever someone wants you to "pay now, it's gone after today", stop, wait a day, and say it out loud to one person. What a scam fears most is exactly that one day and that one person (see Chapter 18).

docs.title: 1.8 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Today, take a sheet of paper and write down one question, for yourself or for your parents:

In the last three months, is there anything about me that has changed for the worse? Weight, strength, walking, memory, sleep, whichever.

If there is, make an appointment and get it checked; don't say to yourself "it's just age, it's normal". If there isn't, keep this sheet of paper, and ask yourself again three months later.

Ask yourself this one question, and you turn "getting old suddenly one day" into "I've been watching it all along".

docs.title: 1.9 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
Of everything in this chapter about "how to say it", the line with the best chance of getting through is to state your own worry, not to tell them they can't cope.

  • How to say this out loud to them: don't start from the fact that they are "old" — they will shut the door at once. Start from one small thing you have seen, and put it as your own worry: "I've noticed you need to hold the wall going up the stairs lately, and it makes me uneasy; I'd like to go with you to get it checked." Say what I see, not what you shouldn't be. You can also use this book as an opening: "I'm reading a book about preparing ahead, and there's one place I'd like to go through with you."
  • When they disagree, what else you can do: there are three things that don't need their nod. ① Write down the "should-be-checked" items from 1.6 (no energy, feeling cold, dizziness, breathlessness, weight loss), and next time you have a chance to go with them to the doctor, tell the doctor about these. ② If they say checkups are pointless, don't push them to do everything; instead, ask the doctor which items are genuinely worth doing for their age and sex. ③ If they have bought an expensive package or health products, don't tear it up in front of them; first ask "who recommended this", then calmly tell them the "starts with a free trial" spotting method.

docs.title: 1.10 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• There is no routine official figure for healthy life expectancy. The National Health Commission's annual bulletin publishes only average life expectancy (79 years in 2024, 79.25 years at the end of 2025) and does not list separately "the years you can get by on your own, without depending on others"; the World Health Organization has estimates of healthy life expectancy for each country, but they use a different scope and method from the domestic bulletin, so they cannot be directly subtracted. This chapter therefore does not use that difference. Next step: if the National Health Commission brings it into its regular annual publication, add it then.
  • Prevalence varies with the diagnostic criteria, so only a range can be given. Frailty: using the Fried phenotype, on the CHARLS 2011—2012 baseline, it is 7.0% among people over 60 third-party research Wu et al., 2018; using the frailty index (FI) instead, for older people in China it was 18.7%, 20.6%, and 28.4% in 2011, 2013, and 2015 third-party research Chinese Journal of Epidemiology, 2018. Sarcopenia: the meta-analysis gives 14.6%, while individual studies range from single digits to thirty percent. The difference lies in the diagnostic criteria, the sampled population, and "which diseases count" — whenever you see any single number, don't take it as a national verdict.
  • The list of things "taken for old age" is an example, not an exhaustive one. The hypothyroidism, anaemia, heart failure, depression, and weight loss picked in 1.6 are the ones most often mistaken for aging; in geriatric medicine this list is open-ended, and there is no "one number" to check it against. The doctor's judgement, made with your specific situation, is what counts.

One honest thing: some changes really can't be turned back. Everyone comes at last to Stage Four, and no one can stop that. What this book can do is make the first three stages slower and steadier.

docs.title: Chapter 2 · Bone and Muscle Capital: Two Accounts You Can Only Draw From, Never Pay Into
docs.text:
Last winter, your mother stumbled in the stairwell and only kept from falling by grabbing the handrail. She waved it off as nothing. But you noticed: she has got a little shorter over these past two years, and her hands aren't steady when she carries things.

You assume this is just "getting old". In fact there are two accounts she never paid into enough back then, and now she draws them down year by year.

This book keeps four accounts, and the first one is independence. Being able to walk on your own, get up on your own, carry things on your own — that rests on two accounts: bone and muscle. This chapter covers three things: how to tell how much you have left, where you can top up today, and when you should see a doctor instead of just pushing through on your own.

docs.title: 2.1 These two accounts are the exact opposite of a savings account
docs.text: Money can be saved late in life; bone and muscle can't. Both have a window, up to roughly age thirty: eat right and move enough before then, and the account grows year by year. Past that window, less and less goes in and more and more comes out. The question isn't "what do I do once I'm old" — it's "how much can I still put in now".

docs.title: 2.2 Bone capital: it tops out in your thirties, then only goes out
docs.text:
Bone grows your whole life, reaching its peak around age thirty — this is peak bone mass. After thirty to thirty-five it starts to decline (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission, "Strengthen Your Bones, Refuse 'Osteoporosis'" 2023; Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025). The higher the peak and the later it comes, the more you can draw on for the rest of your life.

Why it declines: bone contains two sets of cells, one that tears down old bone and one that builds new bone. When you're young, building outruns tearing down; after thirty, tearing down overtakes it. The trabeculae — the spongy struts inside bone — thin out and grow sparse, and the bone turns brittle.

Women lose the most at menopause. Oestrogen normally holds the brake on the "bone-tearing" cells; after menopause it plunges, and bone is lost fastest in the first five to ten years after menopause, at 2 to 3 percent a year (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）); third-party research Xinhua Net 2025). Men lose bone too, just more slowly and later: prevalence in men over 65 is 10.7 percent, with gonadal function declining after 70 (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission 2023).

The numbers for China: prevalence over age 50 is 19.2 percent (women 32.1, men 6.9); over age 65, 32 percent (women 51.6, men 10.7); and among people over 40, 40.9 percent already have low bone mass (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission 2023; Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025).

One honest thing: half your foundation is genetic, and you can't change that; whether you lose bone fast or slow is half in your own hands.

docs.title: 2.3 Muscle capital: it peaks at thirty too, and falls faster after sixty
docs.text:
Muscle mass generally peaks around the thirties or forties, then declines year by year. How fast varies by source: one popular-science piece says it peaks at 30, then drops 1 to 2 percent a year, accelerating after 60 (third-party research China Food and Drug Network 2022); another article reviewed by the Chinese Medical Association says that after 50, leg muscle mass falls 1 to 2 percent a year and muscle strength 1.5 to 5 percent a year (third-party research Xinhua Net 2024). The two sources don't fully agree on the peak age or the rate, but they agree on the direction: past the peak it declines every year, and faster after 60. Drop far enough and it becomes a disease called sarcopenia; among community-dwelling older people in China prevalence runs 8.9 to 38.8 percent, reaching 67.1 percent over age 80 (third-party research Xinhua Net 2024).

Once the muscle on your legs thins you walk unsteadily, walking unsteadily makes you fall, and a fall puts you in bed for three months and costs you still more muscle — the same loop as the falls loop in Chapter 5. Be careful with the old saying "you can't buy leanness in old age": thin is not the goal, and being underweight is itself a risk factor (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）)).

docs.title: 2.4 A rough self-test at home: grip strength, walking speed, calf circumference
docs.text:
• What it costs: basically nothing; a grip dynamometer is optional (Money: barely any money ｜ Time: ten minutes ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: these three numbers are the screening method set by the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia — screen roughly at home first, and leave the formal judgment to a doctor.
  • What you can do: ① Grip strength: with your writing hand, squeeze the dynamometer with the arm hanging down; under 28 kg for men, under 18 kg for women counts as low. ② Walking speed: walk a straight 6-metre path; under 1 metre per second is slow. ③ Calf circumference: measure the thickest part while sitting; under 34 cm for men, under 33 cm for women suggests too little muscle. ④ The five-question SARC-F questionnaire: take a score of 4 seriously. Muscle mass itself requires DXA at a hospital; below 7 kg/m² for men, below 5.4 for women counts as low (all above third-party research: AWGS 2019).
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ the above are the standard criteria of the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS 2019) (diagnostic criteria). But the cut-offs come from multi-country Asian populations; finer China-specific lines are still being researched, so don't treat this as a diagnosis. Also note: a looser set of figures also circulates online — grip strength under 25 kg for men, walking speed under 0.8 m/s; those are an earlier line used for preliminary screening, and AWGS 2019 governs an actual diagnosis.
  • Who this is for: people who can stand and walk on their own. If you can't grip, get winded after a few steps, or have fallen in the past six months, don't test at home — go straight to the hospital.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I'm not sure whether I can still manage"
  • How this works in China: once you've measured, ask the contracted family doctor team at your community health centre whether it matters and whether you need a DXA scan.

docs.title: 2.5 Resistance training and weight-bearing activity: make your muscles work, put load on your bones
docs.text:
• What it costs: a resistance band costs a few dozen yuan; a pair of small dumbbells or two bottles of water will do (Money: barely any money ｜ Time: 20 minutes a session, two or three times a week ｜ Effort: somewhat tiring ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: making your muscles work against a resistance (resistance training) and letting your body weight press down through your legs and spine (weight-bearing) are the two things that build muscle and bone — walking alone can't make up for it.
  • What you can do: ① Resistance: two to three times a week, working the same muscle again after a day's gap; 8 to 12 repetitions per set, two to three sets; start with legs and back — sit-to-stand, wall squats, band rows, biceps curls, and grip-squeezing all count. ② Weight-bearing: walk enough each day, totalling 150 minutes of moderate intensity a week; brisk walking, jogging, and stair-climbing (if your knees are okay) all load the bone, while swimming and cycling put little load on bone and can't replace them ([third-party research: West China Hospital reprint of the Chinese Expert Consensus on Prevention and Intervention of Physical Function Impairment in Older Adults (2022) (《老年人躯体功能受损防控干预中国专家共识（2022）》); official wording: Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025]).
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ both kinds of training are unanimously recommended by Chinese geriatric-medicine consensus. But swimming and cycling have limited effect on raising bone density.
  • Who this is for: people who can stand steadily, sit and stand on their own, and walk without pain — start from a seated position and your own body weight. If you have heart problems, painful joints, uncontrolled blood pressure, or get winded after two steps, have a doctor look first before you start; while training you should still be able to talk normally.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "my legs are getting weaker and can't hold me up"
  • How this works in China: communities and universities of the third age often run resistance and resistance-band classes and walking groups; ask the community health centre or the community eldercare service station.

docs.title: 2.6 Jumping movements: those with strong bones train with it, those with brittle bones avoid it
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing (Money: nothing ｜ Time: a few minutes at a time ｜ Effort: quite tiring ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: when you jump and land, the ground throws a jolt back up into your leg bones and spine; for bones that are still solid, that "shake" is a signal telling them to get harder.
  • What you can do: if your bones have been checked and are fine, you can start with very small hops in place, or hopping off a low step — keep the dose small and build up slowly. If your knees, ankles, or lower back are injured, switch to landing on the balls of your feet and walking briskly downhill instead.
  • Where this comes from: C ｜ the idea that "impact-type movement stimulates bone" has research support. But how much jumping actually helps bones get harder has no quantified domestic evidence; a 2025 consensus warns that people with exercise contraindications should avoid explosive and high-impact movements (official wording Shenyang Municipal Health Commission 2026, citing the Expert Consensus on Nutritional and Exercise Management of Primary Osteoporosis and Sarcopenia (2025) (《原发性骨质疏松症与肌少症的营养和运动管理专家共识（2025年）》)).
  • Who this is for: the "who this holds for" matters most with this one. People already diagnosed with low bone mass or osteoporosis, or who have had a fragility fracture, should not practise jumping on their own — the impact of landing can crush a bone outright; people with brittle bones should train weight-bearing, resistance, and balance, not jumping. Those who are overweight or have knee or ankle problems aren't suited to it either.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I can't tell whether bone gets harder or more brittle the more I use it"
  • How this works in China: this one is not something to practise, it's something to ask — take "can I jump, can I run?" to an orthopaedics or rehabilitation doctor.

docs.title: 2.7 Calcium and protein: get both from your plate, don't count on calcium tablets alone
docs.text:
• What it costs: a glass of milk, an egg, and a handful of soy products on the table every day — several dozen to one or two hundred yuan more a month (Money: some money ｜ Time: daily ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: calcium is the brick in bone, protein is the raw material for building muscle. Get enough of both from food first — a handful of calcium tablets alone won't rebuild muscle.
  • What you can do: ① Calcium: 300 to 500 mL of milk or yoghurt a day, plus tofu, dried tofu, and bean curd sticks; add rape greens, Chinese kale, and broccoli; small fish and shrimp eaten whole with the bones, and sesame paste, contribute a little too. Drink fewer carbonated drinks and less strong coffee, and use less salt. ② Protein: eggs, milk, fish and shrimp, lean meat, and soy products all count — put a little in every meal, don't pile it all into dinner; if chewing is a problem, use steamed egg, fish paste, or tofu instead. People with sarcopenia need more protein, and how much is calculated by body weight (official wording Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025; Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）); third-party research Xinhua Net 2024).
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ "eat more calcium-rich foods, use calcium supplements if intake is short, and get enough protein" is written into Chinese guidelines and the older-adult nutrition consensus. But how much to take daily, whether to use calcium tablets, and how many grams of protein all have to be decided by a doctor, taking diet, blood tests, and kidney function into account.
  • Who this is for: most people. People with kidney stones, poor kidney function, or high blood calcium are different: they must be especially cautious about calcium supplementation and can't eat a lot of protein either — ask a doctor first.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "my bone is draining away and I don't know what to put in my mouth"
  • How this works in China: first go to a hospital for a bone-density scan and a kidney-function test, then decide what to eat and what to supplement. Where to ask: the community health centre, or the hospital's endocrinology or orthopaedics department; if there's a nutrition clinic, have the doctor calculate by body weight. Don't buy calcium tablets on your own from advertising.

docs.title: 2.8 Vitamin D: sun the right time of day, sun the right body parts
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing (Money: nothing ｜ Time: a few times a week, ten-odd minutes each ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: for calcium to get into bone, vitamin D has to help carry it. It's made mainly by your own skin from sunlight, and there's almost none in food; if you get little sun, the calcium you eat won't stay either.
  • What you can do (per national guidelines): ① From early summer to late autumn, sunbathe between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.; ② bare your arms and legs to the sun directly, don't sit behind glass, and don't apply thick sunscreen; ③ 15 to 30 minutes at a time, two to three times a week; ④ In northern winters, the plum-rain season, or for people indoors all day, sun exposure isn't enough and you have to supplement actively — the recommendation is 600 international units a day for people over 65 (600 IU, equal to 15 micrograms) ([official wording: Shenyang Municipal Health Commission 2026; Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025; Chinese Nutrition Society, Dietary Reference Intakes for Chinese Residents (2023 edition) (《中国居民膳食营养素参考摄入量（2023版）》)]).
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ "get sun first, supplement if that's not enough" is written into China's dietary reference intakes; the time of day for sun comes from a domestic clinical expert consensus.
  • Who this is for: most people. People already taking a vitamin D supplement, or with high blood calcium, shouldn't stack supplements on top of each other — ask a doctor; and don't sunbathe until you peel.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I've supplemented for ages and don't know whether it stayed"
  • How this works in China: whether to test the vitamin D in your blood and how much to supplement — go to a hospital for a blood draw and ask a doctor; northern winters are all the more reason to ask.

docs.title: 2.9 Get a bone-density scan, and read the T-score properly
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit plus one scan, 100 to several hundred yuan, varying by place (Money: some money ｜ Time: half a day ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: bone density is the most direct test of how solid your bone is, and the internationally accepted diagnostic method is DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) — not the heel ultrasound at a check-up centre, and not the body-fat scale at home (official wording Healthy China, "Four Groups Advised to Have a Bone-Density Test" 2025).
  • What you can do: ① Who should be tested: anyone over 50 who has had a fracture; women over 65 and men over 70; postmenopausal women up to 65 and men 50 to 70 who have risk factors (such as lower-back pain after activity, being more than 3 cm shorter than in youth, or a stoop); and people taking bone-damaging drugs or with related diseases (official wording Healthy China 2025). ② Where to test: have the endocrinology, orthopaedics, or geriatrics department at a hospital order a DXA, scanning both the lumbar spine and the hip — testing only one site easily misses it. ③ T-score: not below −1.0 is normal; between −1.0 and −2.5 is low bone mass; −2.5 and below is osteoporosis (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）)).
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ DXA diagnosis of osteoporosis is the international standard, and the T-score cut-offs are written into Chinese guidelines. But don't read the report yourself — a doctor has to judge it together with symptoms and medical history (third-party research Xinhua Net 2025).
  • Who this is for: the four groups above; those already diagnosed and on medication should be re-tested on the schedule the doctor sets — don't stop or adjust it yourself. A normal bone density doesn't mean you won't fracture, and the whole fall-prevention routine (Chapter 5) still applies.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I don't know whether my bones are up to it"
  • How this works in China: first get an order or referral from your contracted family doctor at the community health centre, then have the DXA done at a large hospital; in some cities a community check-up can do an ultrasound bone-density screen first, and those with a problem are referred for DXA (official wording Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025); if you've signed up with a family doctor you can get regular follow-up and re-test reminders. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 2.10 Smoking, drinking, and sitting still all draw down your bone capital early
docs.text:
• What it costs: nothing — it's about changing habits (Money: nothing ｜ Time: long-term ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: these two accounts — one is being paid into, the other can be drawn down by a few habits. Smoking, heavy drinking, and sitting from morning to night are three ways you draw down early.
  • What you can do: ① Smoking: what's in smoke damages bone cells and also worsens calcium absorption — quitting is the same act for your bones and your lungs. ② Alcohol: drinking too much damages bone and also makes you unsteady on your feet, more likely to fall. ③ Sitting: get up and move a few minutes every hour you sit.
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ "smoking, heavy drinking, and little physical activity" are listed in black and white as controllable risk factors in China's osteoporosis guideline (official wording Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Guidelines for Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）)). But there's no precise figure for how much bone mass you can claw back by changing them.
  • Who this is for: it applies to anyone with these habits; when you can't change much, start with "stand up and walk for two minutes every hour you sit" — easier to keep than a grand "quit for good" goal.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I'm topping up and leaking at the same time, and I don't know it"
  • How this works in China: if you want to quit smoking, ask your community family doctor whether there's a cessation clinic or a referral.

docs.title: 2.11 If these things show up, see a doctor first — don't just train
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit (Money: the price of one registration ｜ Time: half a day ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: yes, easy)
  • In short: some signals mean the bone or muscle problem has moved past the "just train a bit and it'll be fine" stage — let a doctor sort it out first, then talk about how to move.
  • What you can do — go if you see these: ① Unexplained bone pain: pain at night, or pain whenever you exert yourself, especially lower-back pain. ② Weight loss: a clear, rapid drop in weight. ③ Fracture history: a fracture after age 50. ④ Losing more than 3 cm of height, or starting to stoop. When you go, say clearly where it hurts, for how long, whether you've fallen, and what medication you take, and ask the doctor to assess bone density, vitamin D, and kidney function.
  • Where this comes from: A ｜ these signals are written into China's osteoporosis guideline; treat them as a reason to "go get checked once", not as you diagnosing yourself.
  • Who this is for: anyone with any one of the above. Note: sudden severe bone pain, or being unable to move after a fall, doesn't fall under this — that's an emergency, call 120 (China's ambulance number) per Chapter 5.
  • What you get back: independence + money — no more fearing "a small problem dragging into a big one, and worrying about wasting money"
  • How this works in China: register at a hospital's orthopaedics, endocrinology, or geriatrics department; people over 65 get one free health-management check a year (National Basic Public Health Service), which includes a health-status assessment — ask the community health centre.

docs.title: 2.12 How this works in China: fold your bone density into the community's annual check-up
docs.text:
• What it costs: no extra cost (Money: nothing ｜ Time: once ｜ Effort: no strain ｜ Need to ask someone: no)
  • In short: the state has already folded these two accounts — bone and muscle — into community and annual check-ups, so you don't have to grope your own way in from a big hospital.
  • What you can do: ① Over 65: a free health-management check once a year — ask "bones, muscles, and whether I might fall" into it too (official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standards (3rd edition) (《国家基本公共卫生服务规范（第三版）》)). ② Some communities or check-up providers can do an ultrasound bone-density screen, forearm DXA, or quantitative CT first, and refer those with a problem to a hospital for DXA (official wording Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025) — note that the standard items of the free check-up don't include bone density, and whether you can add it or be referred varies by place. ③ Contracted family doctor services are a scheme rolled out nationwide; once you sign up you get a fixed family doctor team that can follow up regularly, remind you about re-tests, and help refer you (official wording Guiding Opinions on Advancing Contracted Family Doctor Services (国医改办发〔2016〕1 号), 2016-06-06).
  • Where this comes from: B ｜ free check-ups and contracted family doctor services are basic services rolled out nationwide. But whether a community can do bone density and whether it can refer for DXA varies a lot by place.
  • Who this is for: people in cities and county towns near a community health centre; in rural areas, ask at the township health centre first.
  • What you get back: independence — no more fearing "I want to go get checked but don't know which door to walk through"
  • How this works in China: go to the community residents' committee or the community health centre and ask three questions: how do I book the free check-up, can you do bone density here, and is there a family doctor I can sign up with. Go by the latest local wording.

docs.title: 2.13 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Today, stand up from a chair without using your hands, then sit back down — two to three sets of 8 to 12 repetitions.

This move is both a test and a training: today it tells you how much capital is left in your legs, and from now on, twice a week, it's money you're paying into that account. From today, remember one number and compare it again on this day next year.

docs.title: 2.14 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
How to say it out loud. Don't say "you have osteoporosis, your muscles are wasting away" — that's a verdict, and he'll go straight on the defensive. Say something specific that he can't argue with: "Mum, I measured it — you're a bit shorter than the year before last, and you walk more slowly than before. That's what worries me. I want to go with you for a bone-density scan, and a blood draw while we're there. We'll be back the same day." Put "I" into it and leave the judgment to him.

When he disagrees, what else you can do. Three things, none of which need his nod. First, change the table first: keep milk, eggs, and tofu in the house, a glass of milk and an egg a meal — don't say "calcium", just say "I feel like eating lighter lately". Second, measure without saying anything: while he stands up and walks, count in your head — can he get out of the chair, does he have time to cross the road — note it in your head, don't pass judgment to his face. Third, when you go with him to the clinic, ask the doctor three things on his behalf: whether he needs a bone-density scan, whether he needs a vitamin D and kidney-function test, and whether he can still jump and run. He may not admit it out loud, but his body gives an answer every day.

docs.title: 2.15 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• The specific effect of jumping and impact-type movement on bone density in middle-aged and older adults — I couldn't verify a quantified study in a Chinese population. The direction exists (weight-bearing and impact can stimulate bone), but there's no dose data for a Chinese population on "how much to jump, how long, to make bone harder", so this chapter treats it as "direction established, dose unknown". Next step: check the Expert Consensus on Nutritional and Exercise Management of Primary Osteoporosis and Sarcopenia (2025) (《原发性骨质疏松症与肌少症的营养和运动管理专家共识（2025年）》) and subsequent exercise-intervention studies in Chinese populations.
  • Whether a community can do a bone-density screen, whether it can refer for DXA, and whether the free check-up includes bone density all vary by place. Bone density is not among the standard check-up items of the national basic public health service "older-adult health management"; whether a community can add an ultrasound, forearm DXA, or quantitative CT screen, and whether it can refer for DXA, is up to local arrangements (the Chronic Disease Center of the Chinese CDC, 2025, notes that communities can do ultrasound screening first). Next step: check the free check-up items and referral paths of each province's health commission, province by province.
