docs.title: Chapter 3 · Brain and Senses Capital
docs.text:
The TV volume goes up a notch every year. The family says it's too loud; to you it sounds just right. At the market the vendor has to say it twice before you catch it, and you wave your hand and say, "that's just what getting old is like."

This chapter covers five things: brain, ears, eyes, teeth, feet. They're like five switches in a row on the wall — when one comes loose, it's never only that one circuit that goes bad. If your ears can't hear clearly, you pull back from the dinner table, the card game, the people around you. If your teeth can't bite, you eat less meat and vegetables. If your feet hurt, you can't be bothered to go out the door.

docs.title: 3.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
As you age, the first thing to come loose is often not your legs — it's these five. They look as if each runs its own business, but in fact one leads into the next.

Being hard of hearing, blurry eyes, bad teeth, foot trouble — you tend to write these off as "normal for old age." Some of them can be stopped early; and some changes are your body telling you to go to the hospital that very day, not to wait until next month.

This chapter looks at three things: what can be fixed ahead of time, whether fixing it is worth it, and which kind of change cannot wait.

docs.title: 3.2 Hearing loss and dementia share a hard link
docs.text:
Research shows the link between hearing decline and dementia is solid; but how far hearing loss itself causes dementia is not fully settled.

The Lancet Commission on dementia prevention's 2024 report lists 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia, and hearing loss is one of them. The report models this with population-attributable fractions: push all these factors down, and in theory you could delay or stop nearly half of dementia — that's a modelled expectation, not an observed drop in incidence (third-party research Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, 2024 report). The World Health Organization also states that untreated hearing loss raises the risk of dementia and speeds cognitive decline (official wording WHO Deafness and hearing loss fact sheet). The number-one cause of hearing disability in China is age-related hearing loss, at 51.61% (third-party research China Hearing Health Report (2021) blue book, using data from the second national sampling survey of disabled persons in 2006).

One distinction to keep clear: correlation is not causation. People with poor hearing have more dementia — that is observed over and over; but the report itself writes that some of these associations "may only be partly causal."

So does managing it early lower the risk? The hardest evidence is the ACHIEVE trial (2023, The Lancet): 977 people aged 70 to 84 with untreated hearing loss, split into a group given hearing aids plus hearing rehabilitation and a group given only health education, followed for 3 years (third-party research Lin FR et al., Lancet 2023). Taken together, hearing aids did not clearly slow cognitive decline; among the subset at higher cognitive risk, decline was 48% slower.

One more point to flag: a few years ago an observational study said "hearing aids can lower dementia risk" and it was passed around everywhere; the paper was later retracted by The Lancet Public Health (third-party research retraction notice, 2023-12). Don't treat "hearing aids prevent dementia" as settled.

Are hearing aids worth it? The first thing they buy back is "being able to hear, to chat, not to be walled off from the sound of people talking" — that alone is worth it; and the dementia benefit, if any, most likely lands on people who already carry other risk factors (the group in ACHIEVE).

docs.title: 3.3 Get your hearing tested once first, and get hearing aids if you need them
docs.text:
• What it costs: a pure-tone audiometry test runs a few dozen to one or two hundred yuan (varies by place); a hearing aid runs several hundred to several thousand or over ten thousand yuan a pair (money: not cheap | effort: half a day for the test, fitting takes several trips | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: the hardest step — this is where many people get stuck)
  • In short: hearing mostly declines slowly, hard to notice yourself, but the family notices first. Get tested once, get a chart, and then you have something to go on.
  • What you can do: ① register with otolaryngology (ENT) and say you "want to check your hearing," and get pure-tone audiometry; ② have the doctor sort out which type it is — some cases are not aging but middle-ear infection, earwax blockage, or sudden deafness, and need handling separately; ③ when it really reaches the point where you need one, get fitted at a proper hospital hearing centre or a fitting facility with the right qualifications — don't just buy one online; ④ after fitting you need to go back for adjustment and practise using it — discomfort in the first month is common.
  • Where this comes from: B | pure-tone audiometry with proper fitting is standard practice; but the evidence for "hearing aids prevent dementia" only goes as far as "people at higher risk may benefit" — don't treat it as insurance.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people who can hear but can't make out speech, and whose family keep saying you're hard of hearing. If your ear canal is draining pus, you have ear pain, or one side suddenly goes deaf, see 3.8 and go to hospital the same day.
  • What you get back: relationships + self-care — no more fearing "being walled off from the sound of people talking, until eventually nobody talks to me"
  • How this works in China: the free annual health management for people aged 65 and over includes a rough hearing check (official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standard, 3rd edition); for precise hearing testing and hearing-aid fitting, go to the ENT department of a tier-2 or higher hospital. Hearing aids mostly go through the Disabled Persons' Federation's assistive-device fitting subsidy — see 3.9.

docs.title: 3.4 Once cataract affects your daily life, stop putting it off
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit plus one operation; the surgical fee is reimbursed against the local medical-insurance catalogue, and the out-of-pocket share varies by place (effort: mostly day surgery or outpatient surgery | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: cataract is the world's number-one cause of blindness, and the most common cause of vision loss in older people. It can't be treated with pills or eye drops — the clouded lens has to be removed and replaced with an artificial lens.
  • When to do it: not when it "ripens." The National Health Commission's 2026 operational standard says: when the visual function lost to the lens no longer meets the needs of daily life and work, and surgery offers a chance of improvement, it can be done (official wording NHC Operational Standard for Adult Cataract Surgery (2026 edition)). Not being able to see the road and being afraid to step down a stair — you've reached that point.
  • What you can do: ① register with ophthalmology; check visual acuity, slit lamp and eye pressure, and check the fundus if needed; ② ask the doctor three questions: is it appropriate to do it now, which eye, and whether blood pressure and blood sugar need controlling first; ③ if you have high blood pressure or diabetes, get blood pressure and blood sugar steady before surgery, as the doctor says; ④ go back for follow-up after surgery as instructed.
  • Where this comes from: A | surgery is the only treatment for cataract; whether you've reached the point for it and how to do it are decided by the ophthalmologist together with your general condition.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people diagnosed with cataract whose vision is declining. A sudden change in vision, or severe eye pain with redness, may be a different emergency — see 3.8 first.
  • What you get back: self-care + dignity — no more fearing "not seeing the road clearly, afraid to go out, afraid of falling"
  • How this works in China: cataract surgery is a diagnosis-and-treatment item covered by medical insurance; how much is reimbursed, whether it can be done as an outpatient, and whether the artificial lens is chosen from inside or outside the catalogue all vary by place — go by the local medical-insurance scheme's latest wording. Where to ask: the hospital's medical-insurance office, or the local medical-insurance administration.

docs.title: 3.5 When your teeth can't bite, it runs all the way to nutrition and the dinner table
docs.text:
• What it costs: one dental check-up; fillings, dentures and implants differ widely in price, from a few hundred to over ten thousand (money: not cheap | effort: several trips | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: once teeth are missing, you can't chew meat, vegetables or nuts, so you pick only soft things to eat, until your diet grows narrower and narrower. Worse, you start hiding from people when you smile and talk.
  • The current numbers: in the Fourth National Oral Health Epidemiological Survey, people aged 65 to 74 had on average only 22.5 teeth left, and 36.8% of those missing teeth had not been restored ([official wording: Fourth National Oral Health Epidemiological Survey, released by the National Health and Family Planning Commission on 2017-09-20; the figure of 22.5 retained teeth is on the release page, while the 36.8% missing-teeth-not-restored figure is survey detail, second-hand from China Population News, 2024-10-24 — see 3.13]).
  • What you can do: ① see a dentist every six months to a year, don't wait for pain; ② if you have calculus or bleeding gums, get periodontal treatment first, to save the teeth you still have; ③ restore missing teeth promptly: fix them in place if you can; if many are missing and your health is average, a removable denture is also a proper option, and a full denture needs time to adapt and several adjustments (official wording Chinese Stomatological Association, Guidelines for Oral Restoration in Elderly Patients T/CHSA 001-2021); ④ brush twice a day and use floss; take dentures out daily to clean them, and don't sleep with them in.
  • Where this comes from: B | timely restoration, periodontal maintenance and regular denture review are standard in oral-health guidelines; which type of restoration to choose is decided by the dentist together with your general condition and your wishes.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people starting to lose teeth, who can't chew, whose dentures are loose. If you've had a cardiac stent, take anticoagulants, have used bisphosphonate drugs, or have poorly controlled blood sugar, you must tell the dentist before extraction or an implant.
  • What you get back: self-care + relationships + dignity — no more fearing "not being able to eat, eating badly, and not daring to open my mouth to smile"
  • How this works in China: the medical-insurance rules for dentistry vary by place; generally extractions, fillings and periodontal treatment are partly reimbursed, while dentures and implants are mostly out-of-pocket — go by the local medical-insurance catalogue and the hospital you attend. Whom to see: the dental department of a general hospital, a dental hospital, or a prosthodontics department; if your community health centre has a dental department, ask there first. Where to ask about reimbursement: the hospital's medical-insurance office, or the local medical-insurance administration.

docs.title: 3.6 Not being able to cut your toenails is a different matter from diabetic foot
docs.text:
• What it costs: a suitable pair of nail clippers; or one foot-care session, a few dozen yuan (money: costs almost nothing | effort: low | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: as you age, your eyes blur, your back can't bend, your hands can't reach your feet, and cutting your toenails gets hard. Cut into the flesh and it gets infected and fills with pus. If you have diabetes, that one cut can turn into big trouble.
  • If you cut them yourself: ① use large nail clippers with a straight blade; ② cut straight across, leave a little white edge, don't dig the corners in at the sides; ③ soak them soft first, use good light, sit steady, don't perch on one foot; ④ if you can't reach or your hands shake, switch to long-handled tools or have a family member cut them, and if it really comes to it, go to a foot-care clinic at a community or hospital service.
  • If you have diabetes, remember one more thing: your feet are not the same as other people's feet. The Chinese Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Diabetic Foot (2019 edition) state it clearly: diabetic foot is destruction of the skin and deep tissue below the ankle, often with infection and vascular disease; ingrown nails, blisters, bleeding and fungal infections are all its precursor lesions; trimming toenails, nail avulsion and ingrown-nail removal must all be done by trained medical staff, not at a bathhouse or a nail salon (official wording Chinese Diabetes Society, Chinese Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Diabetic Foot (2019 edition)). The same task that's a minor nuisance for an ordinary person can, for you, run all the way to ulceration and gangrene.
  • Shoes and socks: shoes should fit, support the foot and not squeeze at the front; don't go out in open-toed slippers; choose light-coloured cotton socks so a break shows up; check your feet once a day, including the soles and between the toes.
  • Where this comes from: A | the diabetic-foot guideline makes "check your feet daily" and "toenails and calluses handled by professionals" explicit recommendations; for ordinary people, cutting as above carries little risk, but there is no randomised trial specifically on "how to cut your toenails."
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people who can't reach or cut them well; people with diabetes, lower-limb vascular problems, deformed feet or numb feet should not do it themselves — go to endocrinology or a foot clinic. If there's a break in the foot, blackening, redness, swelling, heat, pain, or fever, go to hospital the same day.
  • What you get back: self-care — no more fearing "a small wound on the foot that ends up costing me the leg"
  • How this works in China: high-risk diabetic feet need regular foot checks per the guideline, more often the more severe. Where to ask: a community health centre or a hospital endocrinology department.

docs.title: 3.7 Brain capital is saved day by day: move your body, use your mind, control blood pressure and blood sugar, sleep well, have people to talk to
docs.text:
• What it costs: ten-plus minutes of movement a day; the rest are mostly habits that cost nothing (money: costs almost nothing | effort: daily | strength: not too tiring | do you have to speak up?: no need to speak up)
  • In short: there's no drug that lets you deposit into this "brain capital" all at once — it comes from a string of ordinary things: move your body, use your mind, keep blood pressure and blood sugar under control, sleep well, have people to talk to, and don't leave your hearing and eyesight unattended.
  • How to do it (pick one you can start today):
  • Move your body: brisk walking, cycling, dancing, tai chi all work — accumulate enough each week, don't sit all day (see Chapter 13).
  • Use your mind: read books and papers, play chess, learn something new — this works better than repeating things you already know.
  • Control blood pressure, blood sugar and blood lipids: take your medicine and check your blood pressure as the doctor says, don't stop on your own. This is the most solid evidence, and high blood pressure is among those 14 factors.
  • Sleep well: keep a fixed wake-up time; if you snore loudly, feel sleepy all day, or wake up choking at night, get checked once for sleep apnoea. (Sleep is not among those 14 factors; the evidence is weaker.)
  • Have people to talk to: eat, chat and do things together with people often. Being all alone is also among those 14 factors.
  • Where this comes from: B | that managing several factors together can lower dementia risk is the core conclusion of this report; but which one helps you most, and by how much, can't be guaranteed.
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: people not yet diagnosed with dementia who want to push it off. If you're already clearly forgetting things, or suspect a brain problem, see a doctor first (Chapter 9).
  • What you get back: self-care + relationships — no more fearing "my mind running shorter every day, and in the end not knowing anyone"
  • How this works in China: communities, universities of the third age and senior activity centres often have ready-made classes and teams (tai chi, choir, walking groups). Where to ask: a community health centre, or a university of the third age.

docs.title: 3.8 These changes are signals to go to hospital the same day
docs.text:
• What it costs: one trip out, possibly to the emergency department (money: the cost of one registration | effort: same day | strength: not tiring | do you have to speak up?: easy to ask)
  • In short: some changes in hearing and eyesight are not "slow aging" but emergencies: sudden, one-sided, or with dizziness and unsteadiness. Wait a night, and you may lose something that could have been saved.
  • Go the same day:
  • One ear suddenly can't hear clearly, or suddenly goes deaf. This may be sudden deafness — sensorineural hearing loss coming on suddenly within 72 hours, an ENT emergency where the earlier the treatment the better (official wording Chinese Medical Association, Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Sudden Deafness (2015)).
  • One eye suddenly goes blind, or a black cloth seems to block your vision, or there's a sudden burst of flashes and a marked increase in floaters.
  • An eye suddenly becomes severely painful and red, with vision declining at the same time.
  • A change in hearing or vision together with dizziness, unsteady walking, slurred speech or weakness on one side of the body — treat it as a stroke and call 120 immediately (see Chapter 8 and Appendix D).
  • Where this comes from: A | the treatment window for sudden deafness and the emergency nature of sudden blindness in one eye are both written in the guidelines; remember "sudden, one-sided, with dizziness."
  • Who this is for: who it applies to: everyone. Don't put in a couple of eye drops or dig at your ear yourself and wait for tomorrow. Changes that come on slowly, over months — handle them per the sections above; the moment the word "sudden" appears, treat it as an emergency.
  • What you get back: self-care — no more fearing "something that could have been saved, and I dragged past it"
  • How this works in China: for sudden deafness, register with ENT — some hospitals can add you the same day; for eye emergencies, register with the ophthalmology emergency service; for slurred speech or weakness on one side, call 120. If you're not sure, go to the hospital's emergency-department triage first.

docs.title: 3.9 Where to get these things done in China
docs.text:
• Rough hearing and vision checks in the free health check-up: people aged 65 and over who have lived in the community for at least half a year get one check a year, done at a community health centre, a township health centre or a village clinic; the physical examination includes rough checks of mouth, vision and hearing (official wording National Basic Public Health Service Standard, 3rd edition, "Elderly Health Management"). This is a rough check, not a diagnosis; if problems are found, you're referred to a higher-level hospital to investigate.
  • Rehabilitation assistive-device fitting: basic assistive devices such as hearing aids and walking aids go through the Disabled Persons' Federation's "assistive-device fitting subsidy." All 31 provinces (autonomous regions and municipalities) and the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps have issued policies (official wording China Disabled Persons' Federation / Xinhua News Agency, 2024-02). In most provinces the target group is local certificate-holding disabled persons and eligible disabled children. How much is subsidised, whether you need a disability certificate first, and where to apply all vary by place — go by the local latest wording. Where to ask: the Disabled Persons' Federation at the community (village) or township (sub-district) level, or the county (district) Disabled Persons' Federation.
  • Medical-insurance reimbursement: whether cataract surgery, dental treatment and diabetic-foot treatment are reimbursed, and how much, depends on the local catalogue and the hospital's tier. Where to ask: the hospital's medical-insurance office, or the local medical-insurance administration.

One honest word: of these five, some will keep getting worse all the way. Ears can be partly made up for with hearing aids, teeth can be partly made up for with restoration, and the brain and blood vessels can only be managed bit by bit, day by day. What this chapter can do is stop what can be stopped early, and get the same-day things done the same day.

docs.title: 3.10 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Remember roughly what notch the TV volume is on at home now, and look again next month. The volume creeping up one notch at a time is one of the easiest signals to miss after midlife.

Then, go for a pure-tone audiometry test.

docs.title: 3.11 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
How to say it out loud: don't say "you should get a hearing aid" at the moment when he can't hear you and you've repeated the same sentence a third time — that's pointing it out to his face. Try another way, putting yourself into it: "My hearing's been off lately too — I'm going to get it checked, come with me?" After the test, mention his situation to the doctor in passing. Or leave the hearing aid alone for now and just say "the TV's too loud, the neighbours will complain soon" — giving him a way to save face about turning it down.

What you can still do when he disagrees: what usually trips older people up is "face" and "what's the use." There are three things you can do without his agreement. First, book the appointment and fix the time for him, turning "whether to go" into "which day to go." Second, help him find out how the local Disabled Persons' Federation's assistive-device subsidy works (see 3.9) — lower that money hurdle and the resistance drops too. Third, whether he's willing to wear it or not, start with the "being able to hear" situations: set him up with wireless headphones for the TV, put phone calls on speaker, seat him with his back to the wall at the dinner table and face him when you talk. Once he hears a little better, he'll know for himself that the thing is useful.

docs.title: 3.12 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
The items in this chapter that were marked for verification have all been traced back to source where possible: the two oral-health figures go back to the survey release page and China Population News; the Lancet and hearing-aid passage goes back to the full report and the ACHIEVE paper; the Disabled Persons' Federation assistive-device subsidy goes back to the Xinhua piece on the Chinese government website. The remaining two are limits of the data itself, not things I failed to find, and I leave them as they are:

  • The randomised evidence on hearing aids and dementia is currently mainly just one trial, ACHIEVE, with 3-year follow-up; whether they can really delay dementia over the long term is still unanswered. The observational study a few years ago that said "hearing aids lower dementia risk" has been retracted by The Lancet Public Health and can no longer be used as a basis.
  • Among the causes of hearing disability in China, age-related deafness accounts for 51.61%, from the second national sampling survey of disabled persons in 2006; China Hearing Health Report (2021) was still using this older data when it was published in 2021, and there has been no new round of national sampling since, so this proportion is on the old side.

docs.title: Chapter 4 · Money and Relationships as Capital
docs.text:
On the day you retire, someone throws you a send-off and hands you a keepsake printed with the work unit's name. Three months later, all that's left of the place where you worked for thirty years is a number that lands in your salary card every month — a notch lower than your wage. The last message in the former-colleagues group is a forwarded health article. No one replies.

Those two things are the "capital" of your later life: a pension you have to bank early, and a network of relationships you have to bank early. This chapter is about how to bank those two — while there is still time.

docs.title: 4.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
Part One is called "Building Your Capital". The earlier chapters are about the body, and those all count as "self-reliance" among the four accounts.

This chapter is about the other two: money and relationships.

For the money account, the state has built you a three-tier frame; the top tier is the one you have to put together yourself, and if you never put a hand to it, it stays empty. The relationship account is trickier. It will not sit there and wait for you; it only depreciates. On the day you really need someone to knock on your door, who is still on the list depends on what you have put in now.

The two accounts share one thing: they only pay interest if you start early. Open them when you already need them and it's too late.

docs.title: 4.2 Pensions come in three tiers — first work out which tier you sit on
docs.text:
• What it costs: half an hour, one clear look (money: none | time: half an hour | effort: none | do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: pensions have three tiers. Tier one is the basic old-age insurance the state provides; as of the end of 2025 it covered 1.076 billion people nationwide, and most people's retirement money depends on it official wording MOHRSS 2025 statistical bulletin. Tier two is the enterprise annuity or occupational annuity the employer provides; few employers have one. Tier three is the private pension you save yourself. Work out which tiers you're on first, and only then can you tell how solid the ground is.
  • What you can do:
  • Check tier one: how many years you contributed and how much is in your individual account. Look it up in the "Zhangshen 12333" app, the "electronic social security card", or the National Social Insurance Public Service Platform.
  • Check tier two: ask your former employer whether it has an enterprise annuity; government agencies and public institutions generally have an occupational annuity.
  • Where this comes from: A | The three tiers are an institutional frame spelled out in national documents. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan says to "accelerate the development of a multi-tiered, multi-pillar old-age insurance system", and the private pension comes from Guobanfa [2022] No. 7.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people who have contributed to social insurance and can find their enrolment record. If you have never enrolled, lapsed for years, or work in flexible employment, start by phoning the social insurance agency where you're enrolled: "How do I enrol in my situation, can I make up the gap, and at what standard?"
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "I don't have enough money, and I don't even know how much I have"
  • How this works in China: to look up social insurance, use the "Zhangshen 12333" app or the "electronic social security card" (you can claim it inside common payment and chat apps); for social insurance questions call 12333, or go to the social insurance service hall where you're enrolled. Medical insurance is a separate entrance — use the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.3 The private pension account — if you don't open it, no one opens it for you
docs.text:
• What it costs: one account opening, then a deposit each year (money: voluntary, the cap is set by the state | time: half an hour to open | effort: none | do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: the private pension is "the retirement account you open for yourself": voluntary, you pay in, you buy financial products the state recognises, contributions are deductible against personal income tax, and you can only withdraw at retirement or when you meet the conditions. It sits outside social insurance — an extra tier you add on your own.
  • What you can do:
  • ① First confirm whether you're in the urban-employee or the urban-and-rural-resident basic old-age insurance; either one qualifies you to open the account.
  • ② Open two accounts: the private pension account, through the National Social Insurance Public Service Platform, the "electronic social security card", or the "Zhangshen 12333" app; and the fund account, at a compliant commercial bank.
  • ③ Pay in each year. The current cap is 12,000 yuan a year (set by Guobanfa [2022] No. 7, which states it may be adjusted in time; as of October 2026 it is still this figure) official wording.
  • ④ Choose the products yourself: savings, wealth-management products, commercial old-age insurance, and public mutual funds are all allowed, and since 2024 government bonds are in scope too official wording.
  • Where this comes from: A | The account channels, the contribution cap, the product range and the withdrawal conditions are all written in national documents (Guobanfa [2022] No. 7; Renshebufa [2024] No. 87).
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people still contributing to social insurance, who have spare cash, and who already pay income tax. But it is not a good deal for everyone: the tax you save depends on your bracket, so if your income is low and you don't pay income tax to begin with, there's little to save; and the money runs in a closed account and cannot be taken out early except in the specified cases. Whether to open it, and how much to put in each year, is your own calculation.
  • What you get back: money — no longer afraid that "I have only one pension, and no one fills the gap"
  • How this works in China: for opening an account and looking things up, go through the National Social Insurance Public Service Platform, the "electronic social security card", or the "Zhangshen 12333" app; for tax-break and withdrawal questions, ask the bank where you opened it, call 12333, or call the tax hotline 12366. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.4 Long-term care insurance covers the care bill after you lose the ability to manage
docs.text:
• What it costs: one look-up, one question (money: none | time: one trip to a service window or one phone call | effort: none | do you have to ask: no)
  • In short: the pension covers food on the table while you're alive; medical insurance — China's public health scheme, the rough counterpart of Medicare — covers seeing a doctor. But if one person becomes disabled and the whole family is knocked off balance, who pays that care bill? Long-term care insurance (LTCI) does. It generally doesn't hand you cash; it buys care services for you. In China this is a public social-insurance scheme rather than a private policy you buy from an insurer, and it pays care providers instead of sending money to the family.
  • What you can do: ① First check whether your city runs LTCI. ② If it does, the disabled state generally has to last more than 6 months, and you must apply and be assessed before you can receive benefits official wording. ③ Benefits have no deductible and mainly pay the service fees of home, community, and institutional care official wording.
  • Where this one has got to: it has followed a "pilot first, then rollout" path. The first 15 cities piloted it in 2016, and in 2020 it expanded to 49 cities official wording. By the end of 2025 the number covered had passed 300 million official wording Ministry of Civil Affairs and National Office on Aging, "2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging-Related Undertakings". In March 2026 the General Office of the CPC Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council issued "Opinions on Accelerating the Establishment of the Long-Term Care Insurance System": within about 3 years, by the end of 2028, near-universal coverage nationwide, with the contribution rate unified at about 0.3% official wording.
  • Where this comes from: A | The timeline, the coverage numbers, the contribution rate and the benefit rules all come from official documents (National Healthcare Security Administration, 2025-09-25; Ministry of Civil Affairs and National Office on Aging, "2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging-Related Undertakings"; General Office of the CPC Central Committee and General Office of the State Council, 2026-03-25).
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people already in a city that runs LTCI. Benefits differ from place to place: the national catalogue of service items was only issued in 2025, and the pilot cities will take about 3 more years to align official wording. Another city's rates and services don't necessarily hold where you are.
  • What you get back: money + relationships — no longer afraid that "one person becomes disabled, the whole family falls apart, and the carer's bills drag the household under"
  • How this works in China: where to ask — the medical insurance bureau where you're enrolled, a medical insurance service window, or the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app. Ask three questions: "Does our place run LTCI? How do I apply for a disability assessment? Which services are covered, and how much?" The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.5 What runs out first when you get old is relationships
docs.text:
• What it costs: a little time, one honest look at one thing (money: none | time: one round of asking yourself | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to bring up)
  • In short: when the money runs out there is still the state underneath you; when relationships break there is no one to make it up for you. A partner, children, old friends, neighbours, former colleagues, and a family doctor — these six groups are the real "capital" you can draw on on the day you become disabled. That list never grows by itself; it only shrinks.
  • Why treat it as an account: loneliness is not just "being in a bad mood". A WHO report says about 1 in 6 people worldwide is affected by loneliness, and loneliness is linked to about 871,000 deaths a year official wording. A meta-analysis pooling data on several hundred thousand people found that people with strong social relationships have a survival rate about 50% higher than those with weak ones — the same order as quitting smoking or controlling weight third-party research.
  • What you can do: the ones on this list that genuinely depreciate and need you to top up are the four below.
  • Where this comes from: B | The link between loneliness and health and death risk is supported by a large body of cohort studies; "social connection" is now a WHO public-health theme. But correlation is not causation, and intervention studies on "whether keeping up social ties extends life" are still inconsistent. If you start now, I don't promise you more years; what it protects is this: on the day you need someone, you can still call them out.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: living alone, empty-nest, and people whose social circle shrank sharply after retirement matter most. If your social life is already full, don't stake all your relationships on one group, say only on former colleagues.
  • What you get back: relationships — no longer afraid that "living alone and empty-nested, no one would know, and one old friend after another is gone"
  • How this works in China: at the community level, the places you can use include the residents' committee, the sub-district elderly care service centre, the community elderly care service station, and the university of the third age; what exactly they offer and how to join, one visit and you'll know.

Relationships slip away; you can't stop it. All you can do is slow it down.

docs.title: 4.6 The old-friend relationship needs its own top-up
docs.text:
• What it costs: one phone call and one meeting a month (money: costs almost nothing | time: a few hours a month | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to bring up)
  • In short: colleague relationships are "fed" by the work unit; the moment you retire, the power cuts. Old-friend relationships you have to top up yourself. The older you get, the fewer people you can really talk to, and the few left are worth a lot.
  • What you can do:
  • ① Pick 3 to 5 old friends you can really talk to and fix a set day to meet or call. "Let's get together when we can" means never getting together.
  • ② Phone calls work better than messages — at least one a week.
  • ③ Find something you do together: walking, chess, fishing, strolling in the park all work; a shared activity is what holds up over time.
  • ④ Don't keep it only in a chat app. Put their phone number and which neighbourhood they live in into your phone's contacts, so that if you lose your phone or can't get back into the chat app, you can still reach them.
  • Where this comes from: C | This is common practice and compiled experience; there is no randomised "old-friend maintenance trial" in older people. But the link between social participation and mood and cognition is supported by cohort studies — see the previous item.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people who can still get out and are still up for meeting. If you have trouble getting around or live far away, swap "meeting" for a set call and video. One day an old friend will need you to visit them too; relationships run both ways.
  • What you get back: relationships + dignity — no longer afraid that "after retirement no one looks me up any more"
  • How this works in China: community university of the third age, day-care centre, seniors' activity room, tai-chi group, square-dance team, cards room. Go to the community residents' committee or the community elderly care service station and ask: "What activities for older people are there here, and how do I join?" The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.7 Get to know three neighbours first — in a crisis they're closer than your children
docs.text:
• What it costs: a few nods, one phone call (money: none | time: a few greetings | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to bring up)
  • In short: however devoted your children are, they're a city away. When something really happens — a fall, a sudden illness, a leak, an unlit stove — the one who can knock on your door within minutes is a neighbour. This account is unremarkable day to day and most expensive when something goes wrong.
  • What you can do:
  • ① Start with the people across the hall and two or three households above and below you; know their surnames.
  • ② Leave each other a phone number, not just a chat app.
  • ③ Set a "little signal": curtains open in the morning, lights on at night means all is well; a day with no movement, and you knock.
  • ④ You be the one who knocks too. Take in a neighbour's delivery, lend a hand — relationships are saved up, not handed to you.
  • Where this comes from: C | Neighbourly mutual help is common practice; eldercare in China has long leaned on this informal network of family and neighbours. But not every community has usable neighbourly ties, and new complexes and places with lots of renters are weaker.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: living alone, empty-nest, and people in older complexes (where neighbours still know each other) find it easier. If you live in a new complex with many renters, the more realistic route is to build it through the community, property management, or the building head.
  • What you get back: relationships + self-reliance — no longer afraid that "I'll have an accident alone at night and no one will know"
  • How this works in China: the residents' committee, the building head, the grid worker, property management. Many cities are running visits to seniors living alone and "door-knock" drives; ask the community whether there is one. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.8 After retirement, rewire the colleague relationship
docs.text:
• What it costs: one round of tidying up your contacts (money: none | time: one-off | effort: none | do you have to ask: you do have to bring it up, and it's a bit awkward — you fear being seen as "still angling for connections")
  • In short: on the day you retire, half your social identity goes. Colleagues you saw every day turn into "former colleagues" overnight. This isn't fickleness; it's that the shared thing is gone. If you want to keep them, wire a new shared thing in.
  • What you can do:
  • ① Around retirement, save the contact details of 3 to 5 colleagues you still want to be in touch with; save the phone numbers, don't leave them only in the work group chat.
  • ② Find something tied to your old trade but not to a time clock: re-employment, mentoring an apprentice, a hobby group, an industry old-friends group — let the identity continue in another form.
  • ③ The former employer's events, the retirees' branch, or the retired-staff management office — go once and see if you fit.
  • Where this comes from: C | Compiled experience. "Identity and social-circle contraction after retirement" is a phenomenon geriatric sociology discusses over and over; there is no trial support.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: people who spent a lifetime in a work unit, a government office, or a school find it most pronounced. If you're self-employed, a sole trader, or a farmer, there was no "workplace relationship" to break anyway — for you this item becomes peers, old customers, people from your home town.
  • What you get back: relationships + dignity — no longer afraid that "after retirement I have no identity and have been left behind by the times"
  • How this works in China: the former employer's retired-staff management office, the labour union; an industry old-colleagues group; the university of the third age; some places run re-employment and re-hiring programmes for older people. Go to your former employer's HR and ask what activities there are for retirees. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.9 Sign up for a family doctor in advance, and bank "who to see when I'm ill"
docs.text:
• What it costs: one signing, then on demand (money: in most places the basic package is free or low-cost | time: half an hour to sign | effort: none | do you have to ask: easy to bring up)
  • In short: when you feel unwell at midnight, what panics you most is usually not knowing who to turn to, with no one knowing your background. Signing up for a family doctor is like banking in advance a doctor who "knows you".
  • How to sign up: ① Go to the community health centre or township health centre where you live. ② You can sign with a team or with an individual — allowed under a 2022 policy. ③ The agreement can run 1 to 3 years, renewable on expiry official wording. ④ Bring your ID card and medical insurance card, and ask clearly about the service list and the fee.
  • What it covers: diagnosis and treatment of common and frequently occurring illnesses, and chronic-disease management and follow-up; a referral through your family doctor gives you priority for consultation, tests, and hospital admission; for people with limited mobility or dementia, home visits and a home hospital bed; for eligible chronic-disease patients, a long-term prescription of 4 to 12 weeks official wording.
  • Is it worth it: yes, especially for people with chronic illness, limited mobility, or living alone — it's your "front door" into the hospital. But: the competence of family doctors and the experience after signing vary a lot from place to place, and some places are criticised for being "signed but not served". Before signing, ask: how do I contact this team, how often for chronic-disease follow-up, and how does a referral work?
  • Where this comes from: A | The signing arrangements, the service content, referrals, and long-term prescriptions are all written in national documents (Guoweijicengfa [2022] No. 10). The goal is for contracted-service coverage to reach more than 75% by 2035, and more than 85% of key groups official wording.
  • Who this is for: Who it applies to: most worth it for people with chronic illness, limited mobility, or living alone. If you're in good health and always see specialists at a big hospital, the benefit is mainly convenient chronic-disease follow-up and referral. If you're already disabled or have dementia, use it mainly for home visits and a home hospital bed.
  • What you get back: self-reliance + relationships — no longer afraid that "no one goes to the doctor with me, and I don't know who to call"
  • How this works in China: where to sign — the community health centre or township health centre where you live. Ask three questions: "Who am I signing with? What does it cover? How much does it cost?" For reimbursement when seeing a doctor away from home, ask the medical insurance bureau where you're enrolled, or use the "National Medical Insurance Service Platform" app. The latest local wording prevails.

docs.title: 4.10 The one thing you can do today
docs.text:
Pick up the phone and call the one old friend you most want to keep, and settle on a fixed day right there: next Wednesday at three in the afternoon, a walk together, or a pot of tea.

You can look up your pension any time; that account won't vanish overnight. Relationships are different — they depreciate every day, and today's phone call is the first deposit you make into it.

docs.title: 4.11 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
Every "do it for them" in this chapter works best when it becomes "do it together with them".

How to say it: don't say "I'll look up your pension for you" — say "I've been trying to work out these tiers myself lately and can't get my head round it; help me pull up your contribution record so I can learn from it." Swap "I'll do it for you" for "teach me through it once", and they'll go along. Same idea for asking a neighbour or a family doctor — let them watch you ask.

What you can still do when they refuse: some things don't need their nod. ① You look up their contribution years for them using the "Zhangshen 12333" app or the "electronic social security card". ② Go to the social insurance bureau where they're enrolled and ask how lapses and transfers are handled. ③ Go to their community and ask one question: is LTCI running, and have they signed up a family doctor? ④ If you're not often by their side, help them get to know their neighbours — when you're not there, the neighbours are. These four don't need their agreement; do what you can first.

docs.title: 4.12 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
• "Basic old-age insurance covers 1.076 billion people nationwide" has been traced back to MOHRSS's original release (the "2025 Statistical Bulletin on the Development of Human Resources and Social Security" and MOHRSS's routine press conference of 2026-01-27), and no longer rests on second-hand commentary. "Over 150 million private-pension accounts opened" could not be pinned to an original MOHRSS figure; the only official number is the "cumulative contributions of 145.2 billion yuan" in the "2025 National Bulletin on the Development of Aging-Related Undertakings". The account figures come from several financial media relaying MOHRSS's figures (about 150 million, 2025); when you use them, go by the latest official wording.
  • LTCI coverage moves forward with time and the figures are not fully consistent: the National Healthcare Security Administration said on 2025-09-25 that it covered 190 million people with cumulative spending above 85 billion yuan; Xinhua and the aging bulletin, by the end of 2025, put it at about 300 million. This chapter uses the latter. Implementation timing and benefits differ a lot from place to place; go by the medical insurance bureau where you're enrolled.
  • The link between loneliness and death risk is supported by cohort studies, but on "whether keeping up relationships from now on can extend life" there is a lack of intervention studies targeting older Chinese people.

docs.title: Chapter 5 · Falls Are the First Turning Point in Later Life
docs.text:
Three in the morning. You stand up from the toilet. Your vision goes black and your body tips toward the wall. You catch yourself. You don't fall.

But you know: that instant came close to giving you a different rest of your life. This chapter is written for just before that instant.

docs.title: 5.1 What this chapter is for
docs.text:
This book runs four accounts. The first is independence. Falls are the watershed of that first account.

Before a fall you can walk on your own, get to the toilet on your own, go downstairs on your own. After a fall, many people need a cane or someone's arm from then on, and some never get out of bed again. The difference isn't how much that fall hurt. It's how many years you have left to live on your own.

What follows is not "watch out for slippery floors" talk. It's the moves you can make today, before you fall, and the few people you can go and ask.

docs.title: 5.2 Why one fall can change your whole world
docs.text:
Falls are the number-one cause of injury-related death among people aged 65 and over in China, and the number-one cause of traumatic fractures and of injury-related clinic visits among older adults ([official wording: Disease Control Bureau of the National Health Commission and Chinese CDC Chronic Disease Centre, Core Health Education Messages for Preventing Falls in Older Adults (预防老年人跌倒健康教育核心信息), 2021-10-12]).

Some numbers from China: among community-dwelling adults over 60, about 14.7% fell in the past year; of those who fell, 79.5% were injured (third-party research Chinese Journal of Public Health (《中国公共卫生》), 2021, 21,084 people).

What ends up changing the person is a hip fracture. In China, falls add more than 1 million new hip fractures among older adults every year. It has a nickname: "the last fracture of your life". Six months after the injury the death rate is about 10%–20%, and at one year 20%–30%; of those who survive, about 35% never walk on their own again, and 25% need long-term care (official wording Beijing Municipal Health Commission, reposting Beijing Shijitan Hospital, 2023).

The chain links up like this: a fall → a fracture → surgery or bed rest → infection, blood clots, muscle wasting → the longer you lie there the weaker you get → you never get out of bed again. The death is often not the fracture itself. It's the complications of lying down.

So a fall is not the small matter of "just taking a tumble". It is an accident that cuts a chunk off the years you can look after yourself. And it can be prevented in advance.

docs.title: 5.3 The stool by the door is the cheapest piece of fall-proof furniture in the home
docs.text:
• What it costs: one or two hundred yuan, done in one go (money: hardly anything | time: one hour | effort: none | asking anyone: not needed)
  • In short: Standing to put on shoes, lifting one foot, is one of the easiest ways to lose your balance. Sit down on a stool to change shoes, and that movement is gone.
  • What you can do: ① get a stool with a back and no wheels; ② mount a vertical grab bar on the wall beside it, so your hand has something to push against as you stand; ③ keep the shoes you wear most at a height you can reach without stretching, not on the bottom shelf.
  • Where this comes from: C | common practice. Falls often happen when you turn, bend, or balance on one foot, but no randomised trial has tested a shoe stool on its own.
  • Who this is for: people who can still walk on their own. If you already use a walker, standing up and turning need their own grab bars.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "falling and never getting up again"
  • How this works in China: Shoe stools, grab bars, and non-slip mats are usually on the government's recommended list for age-friendly home renovation (Minfa [2020] No. 86). Go to your residents' committee or the sub-district office's eldercare service desk and ask: "How do I apply for a home age-friendly renovation, and does a case like mine qualify for a subsidy?"

docs.title: 5.4 Renovate four things in the bathroom: grab bars, non-slip, a seat for washing, night lights
docs.text:
• What it costs: grab bars and non-slip work run from a few dozen yuan to a few hundred; a commode chair, a shower chair, and night lights are extra; the total per household varies widely (money: some | time: a few days | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Home is where older people fall most, and the bathroom and the entryway are the two corners of the home where falls happen most. They're wet and slippery, and there you also have to turn, crouch, and stand on one foot.
  • What you can do: ① put a grab bar beside the toilet and another in the shower, fixed into the wall, not a suction-cup type; ② make the floor non-slip and get the bath mats out of the house; ③ replace showering with a shower chair you can sit on; ④ install motion-sensor night lights along the whole route from bed to toilet, not just one lamp; ⑤ convert a squat toilet to a seated one, or add a commode chair.
  • Where this comes from: B | the World Health Organization lists "home assessment and modification" as one of the measures to prevent falls in older adults; which part you change and how much it helps depends on the home.
  • Who this is for: most older adults living at home. Grab bars have to go into a load-bearing wall; find a qualified installer and don't just drill expansion bolts in yourself.
  • What you get back: independence and dignity — you stop fearing "falling on a night trip to the toilet, and being seen"
  • How this works in China: The list in Minfa [2020] No. 86 splits into a "basic" category and an "optional" category. Seven basic items are subsidised by the government for older households in difficulty that qualify: non-slip treatment, level-difference treatment, a bedside rail, grab bars, a shower chair, a cane, and an anti-wandering device. The amounts differ by locality. In Guangzhou, qualifying households get up to 3,000 / 1,500 / 1,000 yuan per household depending on the category of the recipient; ask your district civil affairs bureau or community for the local figure. If you're paying yourself, ask the installer three questions first: did the grab bars go into the wall; is the floor non-slip when it's wet; do the night lights run the whole way from bed to toilet.

docs.title: 5.5 Take a sheet of paper and walk the home spot by spot
docs.text:
• What it costs: one pen, half an hour (money: nothing | time: half an hour | effort: none | asking anyone: not needed)
  • In short: The things that trip you are things you look at every day, so you no longer see them. Put on a pair of spot-the-problem eyes and go room by room.
  • What you can do: go through the checklist below, ticking off each spot as you pass it.
  • Floor: bath mats, thresholds, furniture glides, trailing cords, curled carpet edges, wet patches
  • Lighting: is it bright enough, are the switches somewhere you can reach, is there light the whole way from the bedside to the toilet
  • Passageways: is the hallway cluttered, is there room to turn between the furniture
  • Seating: are the bed and sofa too soft or too low, so that once you sit down you can't get up
  • Reaching things: do the things you use often need you to stretch, stand on a stool, or bend deep to reach
  • Stairs: are the steps a consistent height, is there a handrail, can you see the step edges clearly
  • Bathroom: see the previous item
  • Where this comes from: B | the checklist is drawn from official fall-prevention material and home-hazard risk assessment forms; fixing things one by one lowers risk, but no trial has tested "the checklist itself".
  • Who this is for: everyone. If you already use a walker, measure the hallway width and the turning points separately.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "the house is full of mines and I can't see them"
  • How this works in China: the checklist maps to item 9 of the Chinese CDC Chronic Disease Centre's Core Health Education Messages for Preventing Falls in Older Adults; in some cities the community will come to your home to do a "home fall-risk screening" (Chongqing and other places have pilots). Ask your community whether they offer this service.

docs.title: 5.6 Soles need grip, but not softness — grip and a soft sole are two different things
docs.text:
• What it costs: one pair of well-fitting shoes, one or two hundred to a few hundred yuan (money: not much | time: once | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Many people buy their parents "soft-soled shoes", thinking softer means more comfortable. The softer and thicker the sole, the duller the foot's sense of the ground and the slower the brain's response. Grip comes from the tread pattern; steadiness comes from a sole that doesn't collapse.
  • What you can do: ① a sole with clear tread and grooves grips well; ② some thickness and moderate firmness support the foot; ③ an enclosed heel, no backless slippers outdoors; ④ secure the fit with a buckle or laces tied tight; ⑤ the right size, with a little room from your toes to the front; ⑥ try shoes on in the evening, when your feet are most swollen, so the size you pick still fits during the day.
  • Where this comes from: C | the Chinese CDC put "low heel, non-slip, well-fitting" into its core messages; overseas research on shoes and falls is mixed, but what points the same way is "well-fitting, low heel, supportive". Don't believe that "one particular sole is always best".
  • Who this is for: people who can still walk on their own. If your feet are numb, you have diabetic foot, or your foot has changed shape, see a doctor or a foot-and-ankle specialist first, then choose shoes.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "being tripped by a badly fitting shoe"
  • How this works in China: buy shoes according to item 6 of the Chinese CDC Chronic Disease Centre's Core Health Education Messages for Preventing Falls in Older Adults; don't pay extra for the words "non-slip" or "for the elderly" on the packaging (a manufacturer's claim is not evidence).

docs.title: 5.7 Three kinds of training, each doing its part: strength holds you up, balance keeps you steady, gait keeps you from tripping
docs.text:
• What it costs: ten-odd minutes a day, done long term (money: nothing | time: daily | effort: a bit tiring | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: In the split second when you're about to fall, your body relies on two things: legs strong enough to hold you, and a body that corrects itself. These are two different abilities, and you train them separately. Being tripped often while walking is a third thing — the step itself is the problem.
  • What you can do:
  • Strength (holds you up): holding on for support, do heel raises (lifting onto your toes), stand-ups from a chair, and straight-leg back lifts, to work the thigh and calf.
  • Balance (keeps you steady): standing on one foot (start holding the wall), heel-to-toe "tightrope" walking, and a gently swaying "roly-poly" motion.
  • Gait (keeps you from tripping): high-knee marching in place, walking on your heels, walking on your toes, and stepping over small obstacles, to fix dragging feet, leaning forward, and unsteady steps. Principle: hold on first and reduce the support later; sit before you stand; get the movement right before adding load. Warm up before you train, and don't push through discomfort.
  • Where this comes from: B | the World Health Organization lists gait, balance, and functional training among measures to prevent falls in older adults, and among them the evidence for tai chi is the most solid; China's core messages also list these movement names.
  • Who this is for: people who can stand, walk, and sit down and stand up on their own. If you're often unsteady, or you've fallen within the past six months, get assessed by a rehabilitation department or a physiotherapist first; don't just start training. Being so afraid of falling that you stop moving at all is the worst option: the less you move, the faster your physical function declines, and the more likely you are to fall.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "the dead loop of being afraid to fall, so not moving at all"
  • How this works in China: these movements are inside the twelve-character fall-prevention motto of the Chinese CDC Chronic Disease Centre — "exercise, accept your age, adapt the home, treat early" (要锻炼、要服老、要适老、早治疗); communities, community health centres, and universities of the third age often run tai chi classes and walking groups. Where to ask: the family doctor team at your community health centre, or the community eldercare service station.

docs.title: 5.8 Standing up from a chair without using your hands: how many times in thirty seconds
docs.text:
• What it costs: one chair without armrests, one minute (money: nothing | time: one minute | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Whether you can stand up from a chair using only your legs, without your hands, is the most direct signal of whether your legs have strength. Standing up easily means you still have reserves; needing your hands to push means your legs are raising an alarm.
  • How to do it (do this movement): ① sit in the middle of the chair, no armrests, back straight; ② cross your arms onto the opposite shoulders, held to your chest; ③ feet flat on the floor, back straight; ④ after "go", stand up to fully upright, then sit down, repeating, and count how many times you can get up in thirty seconds; ⑤ if you have to use your hands to stand, stop and score zero. This movement itself is the "sit-to-stand practice" you should do every day.
  • What it means: a screening tool used widely overseas (CDC STEADI) gives "below-average" cut-offs — ages 60–64, men below 14 times and women below 12 count as below average; ages 80–84, men below 10 and women below 9; ages 85–89, both below 8 (official wording the US CDC STEADI chair-stand test form).
  • Where this comes from: B | this is a screening movement used widely overseas, with reference lines by age and sex; but the reference lines come from overseas populations, and lines for Chinese people may not match. Treat it as a comparison, not a diagnosis.
  • Who this is for: people who can sit and stand independently. If you feel dizzy or your heart races after doing it, stop and see a doctor.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "having no idea whether I'm still up to it"
  • How this works in China: the sit-to-stand practice is written into the Chinese CDC's fall-prevention motto ("exercise"), and you can do it at home; whether to measure it and what to do with the result is something to ask the family doctor at your community health centre.

docs.title: 5.9 Before a fall, your body gives three warnings
docs.text:
• What it costs: no money, just your eyes and your memory (money: nothing | time: ongoing | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Falls rarely come with no warning at all. Dizziness on standing up, tingling soles, blurry vision — these three often come first. Many people take them for "just what getting old is like" and tough it out.
  • What you can do: match yourself against the list and note when each one happens.
  • Dizziness or a blackout on standing up: standing up from sitting or lying makes you dizzy for a few seconds. It's usually a drop in blood pressure on standing (orthostatic hypotension). Rise more slowly, sit a moment before standing, and make a point of telling the doctor about it when you go.
  • Tingling soles, can't feel the ground: the foot's sense of the ground gets worse, making you more likely to trip or step wrong; it's common in people with diabetes or lower-back problems. Have a doctor examine your feet.
  • Blurry vision, can't see well at night: falling eyesight, cataracts, and badly fitting glasses are all in the mix. Get your eyes checked regularly, go out less at night, and take a light with you when you do. Two more that are easiest to overlook: having fallen once within the past six months, and needing to hold onto something after two steps — these two are high-risk signals in themselves.
  • Where this comes from: B | a drop in blood pressure on standing, and worsening eyesight and foot sensation, are all repeatedly confirmed risk factors for falls.
  • Who this is for: anyone who has had any of the above. A single fainting episode, or a single time you can't speak clearly or one side goes weak, is not a "warning" — it's an emergency. Call 120 (China's ambulance number).
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "my body was raising an alarm and I treated it as nothing"
  • How this works in China: rising slowly, putting in night lights, and getting your eyesight checked don't cost much; to get these checked properly you'll need a hospital, and see the clinic checklist in 5.12.

docs.title: 5.10 These classes of medicine make falls more likely; take the list to the doctor
docs.text:
• What it costs: one clinic visit (money: the price of one registration fee | time: once | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Many common drugs make you dizzy, drowsy, drop your blood pressure, or lower your blood sugar, and the risk of falling goes up. The problem isn't the drugs themselves; it's "which ones you take, whether any are doubled up, and whether the doses are right" — nobody has looked at the whole list for you. Older people often take several drugs at once, and the risks stack up.
  • High-risk drug list (with sources):
  • Sedative-hypnotics such as benzodiazepines and the "Z drugs" (for example estazolam, zolpidem, zopiclone)
  • Antidepressants (especially tricyclics and monoamine oxidase inhibitors)
  • Antipsychotics and antiepileptics
  • Blood-pressure drugs (blood pressure drops on standing)
  • Blood-sugar drugs (low blood sugar brings cold sweats, shaky hands, and blurred vision)
  • Diuretics (losing water quickly brings weakness and unsteadiness on your feet)
  • Opioid painkillers (sedation, muscle relaxation)
  • Aminoglycoside antibiotics (affect the vestibular system and balance)
  • What you can do: ① write out every drug you take, every supplement, and every "folk remedy" someone gave you on one sheet of paper, or take a photo; ② bring it to your next visit and ask the doctor or pharmacist to go through it from the top; ③ when a new drug is prescribed, ask "will this make me more likely to fall?"; ④ before adding a drug, tell the doctor what you already take, to avoid doubling up; ⑤ don't add drugs on your own, and don't stop them on your own.
  • Where this comes from: B | "fall-risk-increasing drugs" is an internationally recognised class, and multiple papers and guidelines agree. Which specific drug to stop, swap, or reduce can only be decided by a doctor. Internationally there are the Beers criteria and STOPP/START tools to screen for inappropriate medication in older adults.
  • Who this is for: people taking sleeping pills, antidepressants, blood-pressure drugs, or blood-sugar drugs, and especially those taking more than three drugs at once. Stopping or switching drugs must be guided by a doctor; doing it yourself can cause something much worse.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "taking more and more drugs, with nobody to help me sort through them"
  • How this works in China: take this list to your community family doctor, to a hospital geriatrics department, or to a pharmacist at a pharmacy for a "medication review"; if you manage your high blood pressure and diabetes at the community level, get the doctor to look at it during a follow-up visit.

docs.title: 5.11 If someone falls, don't rush to help them up; in these three cases you must call 120
docs.text:
• What it costs: the few seconds it takes to judge (money: nothing | time: a few minutes | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: When you see someone fall, the first instinct is to pull them straight up. That pull can displace a fracture or worsen a brain bleed. Look first, ask first, then decide whether to help them up.
  • What you can do:
  • Assess first: call out twice and see if they respond; check breathing, check for bleeding, whether the arms or legs look crooked, whether they cry out in pain.
  • In these three cases you must call 120, and not help them up yourself: ① unconscious, can't be woken, or vomiting, slurred speech, a drooping corner of the mouth, weakness on one side (possible stroke); ② clear, sharp pain, a limb deformed or shortened, or hip or back pain so bad they can't move (possible fracture); ③ headache or confusion after the head hits the ground, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
  • If they're alert and nothing looks serious: help them slowly into a sitting position and watch for a while; don't yank them up.
  • If you've fallen yourself: first move your fingers and toes to see if you can get up. If you can, roll onto your front first, grab something solid like the edge of the bed or a chair leg, push yourself up slowly, then sit and rest a while. If you can't get up, don't force it: shout, phone someone, bang on the floor, keep warm with cushions and clothing, and wait for help.
  • Hurt or not: tell your family and a doctor, and get the cause of the fall checked once. Someone who has fallen once is at higher risk of falling again.
  • Where this comes from: A | this is the handling procedure set out in both the Chinese Ministry of Health's Technical Guidelines for Fall Interventions in Older Adults (《老年人跌倒干预技术指南》)(2011) and the Chinese CDC's core messages (official wording).
  • Who this is for: everyone. If you live alone, write the "one emergency thing" on a sheet of paper and tape it to the wall in advance: 120, the community phone number, and the phone number of your nearest child.
  • What you get back: independence and relationships — you stop fearing "falling with no one knowing, or being hauled up carelessly"
  • How this works in China: call 120; if you have a contracted family doctor, save the number in advance. The handling procedure is in items 12 and 13 of the Chinese CDC Chronic Disease Centre's Core Health Education Messages for Preventing Falls in Older Adults.

docs.title: 5.12 Four things to check to prevent falls: eyesight, blood pressure, medication, bones
docs.text:
• What it costs: one outpatient visit (money: registration plus tests | time: half a day | effort: none | asking anyone: easy)
  • In short: Fall prevention isn't one thing; it's several things looked at together. Bring a checklist with you and the doctor won't miss anything.
  • What you can do: hand this checklist to the doctor and ask them to go through it item by item.
  • Eyesight: check vision, check for cataracts, ask whether your glasses still fit. If you can't see well at night or things are blurry, say so specifically.
  • Blood pressure: measure it lying down and again on standing, to see whether you have orthostatic hypotension.
  • Medication: bring all your drugs and supplements, do a medication review, and see whether any "make falls more likely".
  • Gait and balance: have the doctor watch how you walk and whether you can stand up from a chair, and refer you to rehabilitation if needed.
  • Bones: assess your osteoporosis risk and check bone density (DXA). China has the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Osteoporosis (2022) (《原发性骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2022）》) and the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Osteoporosis in Older Adults in China (2023) (《中国老年骨质疏松症诊疗指南（2023）》) to follow.
  • Feet: look at the feet, look at the shoes.
  • One more question: which single spot at home should be fixed first.
  • Where this comes from: A | this "screen first, then assess, then intervene" checklist comes from the widely used overseas approach to fall assessment (CDC STEADI), and China's core messages cover the same direction.
  • Who this is for: everyone; people who have fallen within the past six months, walk unsteadily, or take several drugs should go even more. If you can't cover it all in one visit, two visits is fine too.
  • What you get back: independence — you stop fearing "not knowing where to start"
  • How this works in China: book a geriatrics, rehabilitation, or general-practice outpatient appointment; everyone aged 65 and over gets a free annual health-management check, which includes a physical examination (a rough check of the mouth, eyesight, hearing, and movement) plus health guidance on falls and osteoporosis — ask your community health centre about the exact items (National Basic Public Health Service Specification (国家基本公共卫生服务规范), third edition). Bone density and rehabilitation assessments usually require referral to a higher-level hospital. Who does the assessment is up to the doctor, with the family doctor team following up in between.

docs.title: 5.13 If you are reading this for a parent
docs.text:
Your hardest part is usually not knowing that falls need preventing. It's getting him to accept the changes.

There are three things you can do without his approval: ① start with the entryway and the bathroom — if he won't agree to grab bars, first buy an unobtrusive non-slip mat and a shoe stool and say "it's handy for me to use too"; ② photograph his medications and keep the record — bring it to the doctor when you go with him, rather than letting him tell the doctor himself that "I don't take much"; ③ ask at the community once — how to apply for age-friendly renovation, how the free health check for people over 65 works. Find out first, then decide.

He may not admit it out loud. His body will.

docs.title: 5.14 What I am not sure about in this chapter
docs.text:
This chapter originally carried four items flagged to verify; three have been traced back to source: the fall rate back to the original Chinese Journal of Public Health article, the number-one cause of injury-related death back to the Disease Control Bureau of the National Health Commission and the Chinese CDC Chronic Disease Centre's Core Health Education Messages for Preventing Falls in Older Adults, and "the spots that can be prevented" back to the Ministry of Civil Affairs and 8 other departments' Minfa [2020] No. 86 and the Guangzhou civil affairs official notice. The remaining three are limits of the data itself, not things I couldn't find; I've kept them in honestly:

  • The 14.7% fall rate comes from a sample of 21,084 people across 6 provinces and cities in the 2018 PINDEC project, not a national probability sample, so it may differ from the national figure.
  • The "below-average" reference lines for the chair-stand test come from a US population (CDC STEADI); China has no corresponding age- and sex-specific reference values, so they can only serve as a comparison, not a diagnostic standard.
  • The subsidy amounts and item lists for home age-friendly renovation differ by province and city (this chapter gives one Guangzhou example); the local latest notice governs.

One honest note: some falls can't be stopped. The older you get, the more your balance, eyesight, and muscle decline, and no matter how much you prevent, one day you may still fall. What this chapter can do is stop the ones that can be stopped, first.
